title: ELECTRIC: Evidential Learning-Enhanced CT Reconstruction via Iterative Correction
summary: Here we introduce ELECTRIC (Evidential Learning-Enhanced CT Reconstruction via Iterative Correction), a physics-guided Bayesian formulation. An evidential neural network provides an image proposal and an error-predictive epistemic-uncertainty surrogate. The latter is converted into an adaptive precision field and inserted into a Poisson-weighted MAP update. The resulting image-evidence-precision-reconstruction loop treats prior confidence as a learned state variable of iterative reconstruction. In addition to the formulation and theoretical analysis, we report two simulation studies on image slices from the AAPM Mayo Clinic Low-Dose CT dataset: a mechanism-validation pilot using transparent surrogate estimators, and a feasibility study in which a trained Normal-Inverse-Gamma evidential network drives the full closed loop. On held-out patients, the learned prior mean reduces reconstruction error by roughly 70 percent relative to filtered back-projection, the learned epistemic uncertainty is error-predictive and supports selective trust, and the physics-guided update restores measurement consistency while the adaptive-precision reconstruction matches or exceeds a validation-tuned fixed prior and remains markedly more robust to prior-strength misspecification. Together these results demonstrate the complete ELECTRIC closed-loop pipeline, while identifying formal uncertainty calibration and joint training as the principal directions for future work.

AI.tldr: ELECTRIC introduces a physics-guided Bayesian framework for low-dose CT reconstruction that integrates evidential deep learning with iterative MAP updates, using learned epistemic uncertainty as an adaptive precision field. It achieves ~70% error reduction over filtered back-projection and demonstrates robustness to prior-strength misspecification.
AI.motivation: Low-dose CT reconstruction faces the challenge of balancing measurement fidelity with effective priors. Existing methods either fix the prior strength manually (risking misspecification) or lack principled uncertainty quantification. The authors aim to make prior confidence a learned, adaptive variable within the iterative reconstruction process rather than a static hyperparameter.
AI.method: ELECTRIC combines an evidential neural network (using a Normal-Inverse-Gamma framework) that jointly proposes an image and predicts epistemic uncertainty. The uncertainty is converted into an adaptive precision field inserted into a Poisson-weighted MAP (maximum a posteriori) update. The image-evidence-precision-reconstruction loop treats prior confidence as a learned state variable, iteratively refining the reconstruction.
AI.result: On held-out patients from the AAPM Mayo Clinic Low-Dose CT dataset: the learned prior mean reduces reconstruction error by roughly 70% relative to filtered back-projection; the epistemic uncertainty is error-predictive and supports selective trust; the physics-guided update maintains measurement consistency; and adaptive-precision reconstruction matches/exceeds a validation-tuned fixed prior while being markedly more robust to prior-strength misspecification.
AI.conclusion: The complete ELECTRIC closed-loop pipeline is demonstrated as effective, with the authors identifying formal uncertainty calibration and joint training of components as the principal directions for future work.

title: Noise-Robust Conditional Flow Matching: Generating Clean Samples from Noisy Datasets
summary: Generative models learn the statistical properties of their training data, so high-quality generation depends on clean and representative datasets. In scientific imaging, acquisition often yields noisy measurements, while collecting clean references can be costly, impractical or even unattainable. Training directly on these measurements results in a model that reproduces the corrupted data. This can be circumvented by learning the clean population distribution directly from the noisy data. Conditional flow matching (CFM) combines a simple regression objective with stable training, efficient sampling, and strong image-generation performance, making it a natural framework for this setting. We introduce Noise-Robust Conditional Flow Matching (NR-CFM), an unconditional generator that learns from one corrupted observation per image. NR-CFM provides a closed-form clean endpoint correction for additive white Gaussian noise and learns a data-driven correction for general Gaussian corruptions with more complex covariance structure. Across the evaluated corruption settings, NR-CFM outperforms NR-GAN in most cases and remains competitive with Ambient Diffusion in the high-noise regime. We further evaluate NR-CFM on scientific data at signal-to-noise ratios as low as $0.001$, where it generates plausible particle images from severely corrupted measurements.

AI.tldr: NR-CFM is an unconditional generator that learns clean population distributions directly from noisy observations (one corrupted measurement per image), providing closed-form correction for additive white Gaussian noise and data-driven correction for complex Gaussian corruptions, outperforming NR-GAN and matching Ambient Diffusion in high-noise regimes.
AI.motivation: Generative models trained on noisy scientific imaging data reproduce corruption rather than clean structures. Collecting clean references is often costly, impractical, or impossible, so there is a need for methods that learn clean distributions directly from noisy measurements.
AI.method: Extends conditional flow matching (CFM) to noise-robust training using one corrupted observation per image. Provides a closed-form clean endpoint correction for additive white Gaussian noise and learns a data-driven correction for general Gaussian corruptions with more complex covariance structure.
AI.result: NR-CFM outperforms NR-GAN in most corruption settings, remains competitive with Ambient Diffusion in the high-noise regime, and generates plausible particle images from severely corrupted scientific data at SNRs as low as 0.001.
AI.conclusion: Conditional flow matching provides an effective and stable framework for learning clean distributions from noisy data, addressing a key bottleneck in scientific imaging where clean references are often unavailable.

title: PhysAgent: A Multi-Agent Framework for Reliable Remote Heart Rate Estimation
summary: Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) enables non-contact heart-rate estimation from facial videos, but its weak physiological signal is easily corrupted by motion, illumination changes, occlusion, skin-appearance variation, and device noise. Existing rPPG methods typically rely on a single model to directly predict heart rate or recover pulse waveforms, while different strong estimators may produce conflicting yet individually plausible candidates for the same video. To resolve these conflicts, we propose PhysAgent, an inference-time multi-agent candidate-verification framework. Unlike direct prediction approaches, PhysAgent neither trains a new base rPPG model nor asks Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to output heart rate directly. In contrast, it treats outputs from multiple base estimators as physiological hypotheses to be verified and uses a lightweight 4B MLLM, Qwen3-VL-4B, to drive multi-agent reasoning over video conditions, signal reliability, and candidate disagreement. A deterministic physiological verifier checks the fusion proposal, and a reproducible numerical fusion process produces the final heart rate. Experimental results on multiple public rPPG benchmarks show that PhysAgent improves fusion stability and reliability across different datasets and source-domain settings, while avoiding the irreproducibility and physiological inconsistency of direct MLLM prediction or unconstrained ensemble fusion. The code will be released soon.

AI.tldr: PhysAgent is an inference-time multi-agent candidate-verification framework for remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) that resolves conflicts between multiple base heart-rate estimators using a lightweight 4B MLLM for reasoning and a deterministic physiological verifier for final fusion, improving stability and reliability without training new base models.
AI.motivation: Existing rPPG methods rely on single models that struggle with noise from motion, illumination, occlusion, and device artifacts, while different strong estimators can produce conflicting yet plausible heart-rate candidates for the same video. There is no principled way to resolve these conflicts at inference time.
AI.method: PhysAgent treats outputs from multiple base rPPG estimators as physiological hypotheses to be verified. A lightweight 4B MLLM (Qwen3-VL-4B) drives multi-agent reasoning over video conditions, signal reliability, and candidate disagreement. A deterministic physiological verifier checks the fusion proposal, and a reproducible numerical fusion process produces the final heart rate.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple public rPPG benchmarks show improved fusion stability and reliability across different datasets and source-domain settings, while avoiding irreproducibility and physiological inconsistency seen in direct MLLM prediction or unconstrained ensemble fusion.
AI.conclusion: PhysAgent demonstrates that an inference-time multi-agent verification approach can effectively reconcile conflicting candidate predictions in rPPG without training new base models, offering a reproducible and physiologically consistent fusion strategy.

title: SafeBuild-Bench: A Temporal-Robust Construction Safety Benchmark with Graph-Enhanced Data Mining
summary: Construction-safety models must handle concrete deployment risks, such as a worker standing near a scaffold edge without guardrails, rather than only recognize common objects in curated images. Yet real inspection archives are redundant, long-tailed, and collected across changing sites and months. We introduce SafeBuild-Bench, a metadata-driven benchmark for evaluating multimodal large language models on construction safety under realistic temporal and site variation. It is mined from 100K+ industrial image-text records and contains 3,314 task instances from over 3,000 expert-verified images, covering multiple-choice hazard identification and free-form hazard description. To make expert verification scalable, we develop GEMS, a graph-enhanced multimodal selection pipeline that combines a proxy-model confusion signal with graph-based diversity to identify informative candidates from redundant streams. On public instruction-tuning data, GEMS-selected subsets preserve robustness-oriented performance under small data budgets. On SafeBuild-Bench, current MLLMs remain far from reliable construction-safety understanding, with the best overall score near 60. We release the benchmark, evaluation scripts, and GEMS codebase at https://github.com/safebuild/gems.

AI.tldr: SafeBuild-Bench is a metadata-driven benchmark for evaluating multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on construction safety, mined from 100K+ industrial records with 3,314 task instances across 3,000+ expert-verified images. It covers multiple-choice hazard identification and free-form hazard description under realistic temporal and site variation. The paper also introduces GEMS, a graph-enhanced multimodal selection pipeline for scalable expert verification, and shows that current MLLMs achieve only ~60% best accuracy, remaining far from reliable deployment.
AI.motivation: Construction-safety models must handle concrete deployment risks (e.g., workers near scaffold edges without guardrails), not just recognize objects in curated images. Real inspection archives are redundant, long-tailed, and vary across sites and months, making existing benchmarks inadequate for evaluating real-world safety understanding.
AI.method: The authors mine 100K+ industrial image-text records to build SafeBuild-Bench with 3,314 task instances (multiple-choice hazard ID and free-form hazard description) from 3,000+ expert-verified images. To scale expert verification, they develop GEMS, a graph-enhanced multimodal selection pipeline combining a proxy-model confusion signal with graph-based diversity to identify informative candidates from redundant data streams.
AI.result: GEMS-selected subsets preserve robustness-oriented performance under small data budgets on public instruction-tuning data. On SafeBuild-Bench, current MLLMs remain unreliable, with the best overall score near 60%. The benchmark, evaluation scripts, and GEMS codebase are publicly released.
AI.conclusion: Realistic benchmarking reveals that current MLLMs are far from reliable construction-safety understanding. The proposed benchmark and GEMS selection pipeline provide a foundation for evaluating and improving safety-critical multimodal models under realistic deployment conditions.

title: Empirical investigation of 3D CT Foundation Models and Unsupervised Adaptation for Head and Neck Cancer Recurrence Prediction
summary: The rapid emergence of 3D CT foundation models has opened new avenues for predictive modeling from CT imaging, offering a compelling alternative to traditional radiomics which is known to suffer from reproducibility issues and sensitivity to acquisition protocol variations. Yet, as these models grow in availability, a critical need arises to evaluate how well their learned representations generalize across diverse clinical settings and whether adaptation to specific downstream tasks is necessary to unlock their full potential. To address these questions, we benchmarked several 3D CT foundation models for predicting recurrence-free survival in head and neck cancer across two public datasets totaling 3,644 patients, evaluating various adaptation strategies and modality fusion mechanisms. Our findings reveal persistent difficulty in identifying features that generalize consistently across different imaging distributions, as evidenced by significant performance drops on external validation cohorts. Ultimately, the integration of imaging features with clinical data remains the most accurate approach for prognostic prediction, though achieving universal generalization across varied clinical contexts continues to represent a substantial challenge for the current generation of models.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks multiple 3D CT foundation models for predicting recurrence-free survival in head and neck cancer across two public datasets (3,644 patients), evaluating adaptation strategies and modality fusion. Results show persistent generalization difficulties across imaging distributions, and combining imaging features with clinical data remains the most accurate approach.
AI.motivation: While 3D CT foundation models offer a promising alternative to traditional radiomics (which suffers from reproducibility and acquisition protocol sensitivity), there is a critical need to evaluate how well their learned representations generalize across diverse clinical settings and whether task-specific adaptation is necessary.
AI.method: Benchmarked several 3D CT foundation models for predicting recurrence-free survival in head and neck cancer using two public datasets totaling 3,644 patients, with evaluation of various adaptation strategies and modality fusion mechanisms.
AI.result: Significant performance drops were observed on external validation cohorts, indicating persistent difficulty in identifying features that generalize consistently across different imaging distributions. The integration of imaging features with clinical data achieved the highest prognostic accuracy.
AI.conclusion: While imaging-clinical data fusion remains the most accurate approach for prognostic prediction, universal generalization across varied clinical contexts remains a substantial challenge for current 3D CT foundation models.

title: Volcanic Clouds Detection through QCNN and Geostationary Satellite Multispectral Imagery
summary: Recent advances in quantum computing are opening new possibilities for Earth Observation (EO) data analysis. Quantum machine learning (QML) approaches offer novel ways to process information by exploiting quantum phenomena such as superposition and entanglement. These capabilities have motivated the exploration of whether quantum-enhanced models can address long-standing challenges in satellite remote sensing, where complex spectral and spatial signals often require sophisticated feature extraction. Among various fields of application, EO data allow the global monitoring of volcanic clouds and are crucial for aviation safety, hazard assessment, real-time eruption response, and evaluation of volcanic impacts on climate. Yet accurate detection of volcanic clouds remains difficult due to their similarity with meteorological clouds, the variability of eruption signatures, and the coarse spectral sampling of geostationary sensors. In this work, the potential of hybrid quantum convolutional neural networks (QCNNs) for the classification of satellite images containing volcanic clouds was investigated. These architectures integrate quantum computational layers into a classical convolutional framework. Two QCNN variants (with 2 and 4 qubits) have been considered to evaluate their ability to classify a dataset of SEVIRI images, including scenes with volcanic clouds (composed of ash, $SO_2$, or mixed components) as well as non-volcanic backgrounds. Finally, the performance of the hybrid QCNN models was compared with that of purely classical architectures.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates hybrid quantum convolutional neural networks (QCNNs) for classifying satellite images containing volcanic clouds from SEVIRI geostationary sensor data, comparing their performance against purely classical architectures.
AI.motivation: Volcanic cloud detection from satellite remote sensing is challenging due to similarity with meteorological clouds, variability of eruption signatures, and coarse spectral sampling. Quantum machine learning offers novel capabilities that may address these long-standing challenges in EO data analysis.
AI.method: Two hybrid QCNN variants (with 2 and 4 qubits) were constructed by integrating quantum computational layers into classical convolutional frameworks, and trained to classify SEVIRI satellite images containing volcanic clouds (ash, SO2, or mixed) versus non-volcanic backgrounds. Their performance was compared to purely classical architectures.
AI.result: The paper evaluates the classification ability of the two QCNN variants on the volcanic cloud dataset and provides a comparative performance assessment against classical models.
AI.conclusion: The work explores whether quantum-enhanced models can improve volcanic cloud detection in satellite imagery, with implications for aviation safety, hazard assessment, eruption response, and climate impact evaluation.

title: Beyond Random Partitioning: Unsupervised Spatio-Temporal Stratification for Cohort Balancing in Longitudinal Medical Imaging
summary: Rigorous dataset partitioning is a foundational, yet frequently overlooked, prerequisite for reliable deep learning in longitudinal medical imaging. Naively shuffling small clinical cohorts routinely introduces covariate shifts and temporal sampling imbalances across training, validation, and test subsets, exposing downstream models to out-of-distribution evaluation. We address this vulnerability with an auditable Tripartite Dataset Analytics Framework that systematically characterizes spatial grid integrity, multi-parametric intensity fingerprints, and longitudinal temporal trajectories, quantifying the heavy-tailed feature dispersion and irregular, episodic sampling intervals typical of real-world clinical cohorts. Building on this characterization, we formalize an unsupervised spatio-temporal cohort-balancing standard operating procedure (SOP) that combines elbow-optimized K-means clustering over a standardized, six-dimensional joint intensity-temporal feature space with intra-cluster proportionate stratified sampling. On a longitudinal, contrast-enhanced $T1$-weighted brain MRI cohort (N=149), the protocol reduces the maximum cross-subset intensity bias from 34.1% under conventional random shuffling to under 2.1%, while aligning longitudinal follow-up intervals closely around the population mean. Monte Carlo stress testing across ten random seeds and three split configurations confirms that this alignment remains tightly bounded, in clear contrast to the substantial variability of random partitioning. The resulting protocol offers a reproducible, generalizable procedure for cohort engineering in variable-length longitudinal clinical imaging workflows.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Tripartite Dataset Analytics Framework and an unsupervised spatio-temporal cohort-balancing SOP (elbow-optimized K-means clustering over a six-dimensional intensity-temporal feature space with intra-cluster stratified sampling) to rigorously partition longitudinal medical imaging datasets, reducing cross-subset intensity bias from 34.1% to under 2.1% on a brain MRI cohort (N=149).
AI.motivation: Naive random shuffling of small clinical cohorts introduces covariate shifts and temporal sampling imbalances across train/validation/test splits, exposing downstream models to out-of-distribution evaluation—a frequently overlooked but foundational problem in longitudinal medical imaging deep learning.
AI.method: A three-part approach: (1) a Tripartite Dataset Analytics Framework characterizing spatial grid integrity, multi-parametric intensity fingerprints, and longitudinal temporal trajectories (quantifying heavy-tailed feature dispersion and episodic sampling); (2) an unsupervised spatio-temporal cohort-balancing SOP combining elbow-optimized K-means clustering over a standardized six-dimensional joint intensity-temporal feature space; (3) intra-cluster proportionate stratified sampling to construct balanced train/validation/test partitions.
AI.result: On a longitudinal, contrast-enhanced T1-weighted brain MRI cohort (N=149), the protocol reduces maximum cross-subset intensity bias from 34.1% (random shuffling) to under 2.1%, aligns longitudinal follow-up intervals near the population mean, and Monte Carlo stress testing across ten random seeds and three split configurations confirms tightly bounded alignment versus substantial variability in random partitioning.
AI.conclusion: The proposed protocol provides a reproducible, generalizable procedure for cohort engineering in variable-length longitudinal clinical imaging workflows, offering an auditable and robust alternative to naive random data partitioning.

title: Explainable Multimodal AI for Adaptive Calibration of Archaeological Sensing Workflows
summary: This paper presents a multimodal machine-learning framework for calibration monitoring, quality assessment, and adaptive acquisition support in archaeological digitisation workflows. The proposed approach operates across photogrammetric 3D reconstruction, hyperspectral imaging, X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy, and Raman spectroscopy through a unified pipeline combining deterministic quality indicators, statistical feature representations, machine-learning classification, anomaly detection, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). Rather than replacing instrument-level calibration, the framework introduces an additional algorithmic layer that evaluates whether acquisitions are statistically consistent, physically plausible, and suitable for downstream multimodal integration. For each sensing modality, acquisitions are represented through structured feature spaces encoding geometric, spectral, spatial, and statistical properties. These representations are used to identify degradation patterns such as reconstruction artefacts, illumination inconsistencies, spectral distortions, detector instability, baseline fluctuations, and low signal-to-noise conditions. Supervised and unsupervised learning methods are combined with XAI techniques to support both automatic discrimination between acceptable and problematic acquisitions and interpretation of the underlying causes of degradation. The framework additionally supports adaptive feedback and resource-aware acquisition strategies by linking feature-space deviations to acquisition-level corrective actions. Experimental results obtained on multimodal archaeological datasets demonstrate that the proposed methodology captures meaningful acquisition variability and enables robust quality assessment across heterogeneous sensing modalities.

AI.tldr: A multimodal ML framework for quality monitoring, assessment, and adaptive support in archaeological digitisation across photogrammetry, hyperspectral imaging, XRF, and Raman spectroscopy.
AI.motivation: Archaeological digitisation workflows involve heterogeneous sensing modalities that need consistent quality control to ensure reliable downstream multimodal integration, but instrument-level calibration alone is insufficient.
AI.method: A unified pipeline combining deterministic quality indicators, statistical feature representations, supervised/unsupervised ML classification, anomaly detection, and explainable AI (XAI) operating on structured feature spaces across four sensing modalities.
AI.result: Experiments on multimodal archaeological datasets show the framework captures meaningful acquisition variability and enables robust quality assessment across heterogeneous sensing modalities.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides an additional algorithmic quality-assessment layer that supports adaptive feedback and resource-aware acquisition strategies without replacing instrument calibration.

title: K-space Gaussian Representation for Parallel MRI
summary: Accelerated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) aims to recover the k-space signal from acquired measurements, where accurate estimation of missing samples is essential for high-fidelity reconstruction. Existing k-space reconstruction methods estimate missing samples through interpolation operators or structure priors defined on discrete sampling grids. Although these formulations effectively exploit local interpolation relationships and global k-space redundancy, they reconstruct only discrete frequency coefficients and therefore do not explicitly model the underlying continuous signal. To overcome this limitation, we propose K-space Gaussian Representation (KGR), the first explicit continuous representation formulated directly in the native k-space domain. Rather than estimating unknown samples on discrete grids, KGR parameterizes the continuous signal using Gabor-Gaussian primitives with shared spatial geometry, yielding a compact representation that naturally preserves inter-coil correlations. Because unconstrained continuous fitting does not necessarily satisfy the intrinsic structural properties of multi-coil signal, the estimated representation is projected onto a low-rank manifold to enforce the algebraic constraints arising from smoothly varying phase and coil redundancy. A frequency-adaptive fitting strategy accommodates the heterogeneous characteristics of different k-space regions. Comprehensive validation across multiple datasets and sampling schemes shows consistent improvements over representative reconstruction baselines in both quantitative metrics and visual quality. These results suggest that explicit continuous parameterization of native k-space provides a principled framework for integrating continuous signal modeling with structured low-rank reconstruction.

AI.tldr: KGR is the first explicit continuous representation for MRI k-space reconstruction, parameterizing the signal using Gabor-Gaussian primitives with shared spatial geometry, projected onto a low-rank manifold, and fitted adaptively by frequency region.
AI.motivation: Existing k-space reconstruction methods estimate missing samples on discrete grids, which fails to explicitly model the underlying continuous signal. This limits reconstruction fidelity.
AI.method: Proposes K-space Gaussian Representation (KGR), which parameterizes the continuous k-space signal using Gabor-Gaussian primitives with shared spatial geometry to preserve inter-coil correlations. A low-rank manifold projection enforces algebraic constraints (smooth phase, coil redundancy), and a frequency-adaptive fitting strategy handles heterogeneous k-space regions.
AI.result: Comprehensive validation across multiple datasets and sampling schemes shows consistent improvements over representative reconstruction baselines in both quantitative metrics and visual quality.
AI.conclusion: Explicit continuous parameterization of native k-space provides a principled framework for integrating continuous signal modeling with structured low-rank reconstruction.

title: Which Modality Decides? Counterfactual Modality Attribution for Multimodal LLMs
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) increasingly support high-stakes decision making by combining complementary information from images and text. While existing explainability methods identify influential image regions or text tokens, they cannot answer a fundamental question: which modality drives a prediction? Consequently, a model may produce the correct output while relying on the wrong source of evidence, masking shortcut learning and unsafe reasoning. We formulate modality attribution as a complementary explainability objective for multimodal foundation models and propose Counterfactual Modality Attribution (CMA), the first framework for quantifying modality-level contributions in MLLMs. CMA generates image-only, text-only, and joint multimodal counterfactuals using coupled diffusion priors and converts them into principled modality attribution scores through a cooperative game-theoretic formulation based on Shapley values. We evaluate CMA on controlled synthetic benchmarks with known ground-truth modality reliance and on a real-world multimodal clinical dataset. CMA correctly identifies the decision-driving modality in 98% of controlled cases and consistently outperforms baselines, revealing failures of cross-modal reasoning that remain invisible to predictive accuracy alone. Our results establish modality attribution as a complementary dimension of explainability beyond feature attribution, providing a principled framework for auditing multimodal foundation models in safety-critical applications.

AI.tldr: CMA is the first framework for quantifying modality-level contributions in multimodal LLMs, using counterfactual generation with coupled diffusion priors and Shapley-value-based game theory to determine which modality drives a prediction.
AI.motivation: Existing explainability methods identify influential image regions or text tokens but cannot answer which modality drives a prediction. This masks shortcut learning and unsafe reasoning in high-stakes multimodal decision making.
AI.method: CMA generates image-only, text-only, and joint multimodal counterfactuals using coupled diffusion priors, then converts them into modality attribution scores through a cooperative game-theoretic formulation based on Shapley values.
AI.result: CMA correctly identifies the decision-driving modality in 98% of controlled cases and consistently outperforms baselines, revealing cross-modal reasoning failures invisible to predictive accuracy alone.
AI.conclusion: Modality attribution is a complementary dimension of explainability beyond feature attribution, providing a principled framework for auditing multimodal foundation models in safety-critical applications.

title: Beyond Accuracy: Auditing Spatial Provenance in Visual Token Pruning for OCR-Critical MLLM Inference
comment: 21 pages, including supplementary material. Code and reproducibility artifacts: https://github.com/SouthWinter/spatial-provenance-audit
summary: Visual-token pruning is usually judged by answer quality at a fixed retention budget. For text-rich multimodal large language models (MLLMs), this protocol can miss a distinct failure: an answer remains correct even when no retained token is locally traceable to the small OCR region that supports it. We turn this blind spot into an evidence-risk audit that couples answer behavior with geometric token-origin provenance, interventions, and realized cost; transparent training-free selectors isolate controlled operating points. On locked image-disjoint confirmation, Qwen Target at 30% retention has observed accuracy 0.786 versus 0.783 for Full (paired image-cluster difference +0.003, 95% CI [-0.014, +0.020]), yet same-budget Target, Random, and Grid retain sharply different positive-support coverage: 0.620, 0.270, and 0.318. Across Qwen3-VL-8B, LLaVA-1.5-7B, and InternVL3.5-8B, matched controls, interventions, detector tests, and external methods reveal model-specific quality-risk-traceability frontiers that accuracy alone does not expose. Materialized prefixes yield up to 4.32x batch-prefill speedup and 76.4% lower incremental peak memory; full-validation TextVQA and DocVQA further show that favorable target-verification points do not imply task-general compression. Visual-token pruning should therefore report surviving spatial provenance and realized cost alongside quality and compression.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a blind spot in visual-token pruning evaluation for text-rich MLLMs: an answer can remain correct even when no retained token is traceable to the supporting OCR region. The authors propose an evidence-risk audit coupling answer behavior with geometric token-origin provenance, interventions, and realized cost. They demonstrate that accuracy alone fails to expose model-specific quality-risk-traceability frontiers, and show that materialized prefixes yield up to 4.32x speedup with 76.4% lower memory, while favorable target-verification points do not imply task-general compression.
AI.motivation: Standard visual-token pruning evaluation judges only answer quality at fixed retention budgets, which can miss cases where answers remain correct despite no retained token being locally traceable to the supporting OCR region. This creates a blind spot in assessing whether pruned tokens preserve the evidence needed for answers.
AI.method: The authors propose an evidence-risk audit that couples answer behavior with geometric token-origin provenance, interventions, and realized cost. Transparent training-free selectors (Target, Random, Grid) are used to isolate controlled operating points, with locked image-disjoint confirmation across multiple models including Qwen3-VL-8B, LLaVA-1.5-7B, and InternVL3.5-8B.
AI.result: At 30% retention, Qwen Target achieves observed accuracy 0.786 vs 0.783 for Full (+0.003, 95% CI [-0.014, +0.020]), yet positive-support coverage differs sharply: 0.620 for Target vs 0.270 Random and 0.318 Grid. Materialized prefixes yield up to 4.32x batch-prefill speedup and 76.4% lower incremental peak memory. Full-validation TextVQA and DocVQA show favorable target-verification does not imply task-general compression.
AI.conclusion: Visual-token pruning evaluation should report surviving spatial provenance and realized cost alongside quality and compression, as accuracy-alone metrics mask model-specific quality-risk-traceability frontiers and can give falsely reassuring results.

title: Device-First Feedback: Toward Mobile-Native LLM-Driven Neural Architecture Search
summary: Deploying convolutional neural networks generated by large language models (LLMs) on real mobile hardware requires more than GPU validation accuracy: INT8 TensorFlow Lite export, delegate selection, and on-device latency jointly determine whether a model is usable. We present an automated mobile deployment pipeline that closes the loop from QLoRA fine-tuning of an architecture-generating LLM through GPU evaluation, INT8 export, and physical-device benchmarking to gated augmentation of the training corpus. The pipeline is fully scripted and runs cycle-by-cycle without manual intervention, with resume support after interruptions. We evaluate the same frozen protocol on two benchmarks, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, on a Samsung SM-P613 tablet (seed 42, 20 models per cycle, cycles 0-6). On CIFAR-10, cycle 1 is gate-accepted and improves the mobile deployment score approximately 25.6x over the baseline with a mean quantized accuracy of 46.9%; later cycles raise GPU accuracy but fail the non-decreasing mobile gate. On CIFAR-100, the pre-QLoRA baseline retains the best mobile score; iterative rounds improve GPU accuracy (up to 26.2%) yet cannot surpass cycle 0 on-device, and the training pool stalls at 19 examples after the first accepted round. Together, the two studies show that closed-loop GPU fine-tuning does not guarantee monotonic mobile gains, especially on harder classification tasks, and that multi-dataset, on-device measurement is needed to stress-test deployment objectives. We release per-cycle metrics with 95% confidence intervals, all figures, and complete reproduction commands.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an automated pipeline for deploying LLM-generated CNN architectures on real mobile hardware, closing the loop from QLoRA fine-tuning through GPU evaluation, INT8 export, and on-device benchmarking. Evaluated on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 across cycles 0-6, the pipeline shows significant mobile deployment score improvements (~25.6x) on CIFAR-10 but fails to achieve monotonic mobile gains on the harder CIFAR-100 task, demonstrating that GPU fine-tuning does not guarantee on-device improvements.
AI.motivation: Deploying LLM-generated CNNs on real mobile hardware requires more than just GPU validation accuracy—INT8 TensorFlow Lite export, delegate selection, and on-device latency jointly determine model usability. Existing approaches lack an automated pipeline that integrates physical-device benchmarking into the model generation loop.
AI.method: An automated mobile deployment pipeline that: (1) performs QLoRA fine-tuning of an architecture-generating LLM, (2) evaluates generated architectures on GPU, (3) exports models to INT8 TensorFlow Lite format, (4) benchmarks them on physical devices (Samsung SM-P613 tablet), and (5) gates acceptance of models to augment the training corpus. The pipeline runs cycle-by-cycle autonomously with resume support after interruptions.
AI.result: On CIFAR-10: cycle 1 is gate-accepted, improving mobile deployment score ~25.6x over baseline with mean quantized accuracy of 46.9%; later cycles improve GPU accuracy but fail the mobile gate. On CIFAR-100: the pre-QLoRA baseline retains the best mobile score; iterative rounds improve GPU accuracy (up to 26.2%) but cannot surpass cycle 0 on-device; training pool stalls at 19 examples.
AI.conclusion: Closed-loop GPU fine-tuning does not guarantee monotonic mobile gains, especially on harder classification tasks. Multi-dataset, on-device measurement is essential to properly stress-test deployment objectives. The paper releases per-cycle metrics with 95% confidence intervals, figures, and reproduction commands for transparency.

title: LeapTalk: Breaking the Latency-Quality Trade-off in Talking Head Generation
summary: Long-form and real-time talking-head generation remains challenging due to a latency-quality trade-off: inefficient multi-step diffusion prohibits streaming generation, whereas real-time autoregressive approaches suffer from error accumulation and identity drift. To address this drawback, we propose LeapTalk, a novel framework that achieves stable and real-time talking-head generation with a single forward step, scaling to arbitrarily long videos. At the heart of our approach lies a single-step bridge distillation scheme. On the one hand, departing from the conventional noise-to-data paradigm, we introduce a data-to-data transport formulation based on a Brownian bridge. Anchored by a persistent reference, this strategy effectively mitigates identity drift and enhances long-term temporal stability. On the other hand, to enable smooth knowledge transfer from a pre-trained diffusion teacher to the student bridge model, we explore a heterogeneous distillation framework with an SNR-aligned time transformation $Φ(τ)$, which bridges the functional discrepancy between the two models. Moreover, we propose an audio-driven classifier-free guidance mechanism to maintain fine-grained lip synchronization under extreme step reduction. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves high-fidelity and temporally consistent video generation with only 1 step at up to 200 FPS, significantly outperforming existing approaches in both efficiency and stability. Project Page: https://zhangrongxiang.github.io/leaptalk-page/

AI.tldr: LeapTalk is a framework for stable, real-time talking-head generation using a single-step bridge distillation scheme, achieving up to 200 FPS with high fidelity and temporal consistency for arbitrarily long videos.
AI.motivation: Long-form and real-time talking-head generation suffers from a latency-quality trade-off: multi-step diffusion models are inefficient for streaming, while real-time autoregressive approaches accumulate errors and suffer from identity drift.
AI.method: LeapTalk uses: (1) a single-step bridge distillation with a data-to-data Brownian bridge transport formulation anchored by a persistent reference to mitigate identity drift; (2) a heterogeneous distillation framework with an SNR-aligned time transformation Φ(τ) for knowledge transfer from a pre-trained diffusion teacher; (3) an audio-driven classifier-free guidance mechanism for fine-grained lip synchronization under extreme step reduction.
AI.result: The method achieves high-fidelity and temporally consistent video generation with only 1 step at up to 200 FPS, significantly outperforming existing approaches in both efficiency and stability.
AI.conclusion: LeapTalk resolves the latency-quality trade-off in talking-head generation by enabling stable, real-time, arbitrarily long video generation in a single forward step.

title: Beyond Edge Maps: Wavelet-Domain Conditioning for Multi-Adapter Map-to-Satellite Diffusion
summary: Commercial mapping partnerships are often unavailable in low-resource regions, leaving satellite basemaps stale and motivating synthesis of satellite imagery from independently maintained cartographic data. Existing ControlNet-based diffusion methods typically condition on structural signals like edges or segmentation extracted from the target image itself, assuming the imagery already exists and limiting their use exactly where synthesis matters most. Map-conditioned alternatives add cues like edge detection but omit frequency-domain structure. We propose a ControlNet-based diffusion framework conditioned only on cartographic sources obtainable independently of the target imagery: OpenStreetMap (OSM) raster maps and their stationary wavelet transform (SWT) subbands, a conditioning signal previously unexplored for map-to-satellite diffusion. Two ControlNet adapters, trained separately on the map and wavelet representations atop a frozen Stable Diffusion backbone, are fused via MultiControlNet, jointly drawing on spatial structure and frequency detail without retraining a multi-input model. We evaluate on a new paired map-satellite dataset curated for Nepal, a data-scarce, topographically diverse region, alongside the Pix2Pix maps-satellite benchmark. Combined conditioning wins six of eight metric-dataset comparisons -- SSIM and PSNR on both datasets, plus LPIPS (both Alex and VGG backbones) on ours and ties map-only on both Pix2Pix LPIPS backbones while still edging past wavelet-only there. Wavelet-only takes the lowest FID on both datasets, matching the tradeoff between per-image fidelity and distributional realism. We treat this gap cautiously given our modest test-set sizes and FID's known small-sample bias.

AI.tldr: Proposes a ControlNet-based diffusion framework for map-to-satellite image synthesis that conditions only on OpenStreetMap raster maps and their stationary wavelet transform subbands, fusing two ControlNet adapters via MultiControlNet. Evaluated on a new Nepal dataset and Pix2Pix benchmark, combined conditioning wins most fidelity metrics while wavelet-only achieves best FID.
AI.motivation: Commercial mapping partnerships are unavailable in low-resource regions, making satellite basemaps stale. Existing methods either condition on structural signals extracted from target imagery (unavailable where synthesis matters most) or add only edge-based cues to map conditioning while omitting frequency-domain structure. This motivates a framework conditioned purely on independently obtainable cartographic data with frequency-domain information.
AI.method: A ControlNet-based diffusion framework with two separate adapters: one conditioned on OSM raster maps and another on stationary wavelet transform (SWT) subbands of those maps. Both adapters are trained separately on a frozen Stable Diffusion backbone and fused via MultiControlNet, jointly capturing spatial structure and frequency detail without retraining a multi-input model.
AI.result: Combined conditioning wins six of eight metric-dataset comparisons, achieving best SSIM and PSNR on both Nepal and Pix2Pix datasets, and best LPIPS (Alex and VGG) on the Nepal dataset. Wavelet-only conditioning achieves the lowest FID on both datasets, indicating a tradeoff between per-image fidelity and distributional realism.
AI.conclusion: Combining OSM maps with SWT subbands via MultiControlNet effectively improves per-image fidelity metrics, while wavelet-only conditioning favors distributional realism (FID). The authors treat the FID gap cautiously due to small test-set sizes and FID's known small-sample bias.

title: From Pixels to PCells: A Neurosymbolic Approach to Photonic Component Creation
summary: We present PixCell, a neurosymbolic system in which multimodal agents convert a visually presented photonic component into a parametric program over a small domain-specific language (DSL) of geometric primitives. A system enabling deterministic visual verification renders evaluation asymmetrically cheaper than the generation attempt. While models using multi-seed sampling and iterative revision reach a mean best-turn IoU of only 0.416, multimodal agents through PixCell's interface and verifier consistently exceed 0.9 mean IoU, with scores reaching 0.974 and 0.955 across eight component targets while also satisfying source contracts. These results demonstrate that frontier multimodal agents can reliably understand and render executable parametric representations from visual targets. Using these live parameters, cross-stack studies on an interferometer reconstruct primitive programs that satisfy an 8.0 nm free spectral range target and the original footprint constraint on modeled 220-nm SOI, 400-nm SiN, and 400-nm TFLN stacks. PixCell further carries a paper-derived splitter from visual reconstruction through SOI full-wave simulation, producing symmetric propagation and balanced outputs. Finally, the same executable verifier supplies a training reward and dataset used to train a Qwen3.6-35B-A3B model with LoRA and GRPO without supervised demonstrations. On eight training-excluded paper figures, its mean champion IoU rises from 0.422 after eight initial attempts to 0.491 after three verifier-guided revision rounds. These results therefore establish a controlled framework for measuring, retargeting, and improving visual-to-parametric photonic component design.

AI.tldr: PixCell is a neurosymbolic system where multimodal agents convert visually presented photonic components into parametric programs using a DSL of geometric primitives. It achieves >0.9 mean IoU (vs 0.416 for naive models), enables cross-stack photonic design, and uses its executable verifier to train a Qwen3.6-35B-A3B model via LoRA and GRPO without supervised demonstrations.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between visual representation of photonic components and executable parametric designs, enabling deterministic verification and reliable reconstruction of photonic devices from images.
AI.method: PixCell combines a DSL of geometric primitives with multimodal agents that convert visual targets into parametric programs. A deterministic visual verifier makes evaluation cheaper than generation. The verifier also serves as a training reward for fine-tuning a Qwen3.6-35B-A3B model using LoRA and GRPO without supervised demonstrations.
AI.result: Multimodal agents achieve 0.974 and 0.955 mean IoU across eight component targets (vs 0.416 baseline). Cross-stack interferometer studies satisfy 8.0 nm FSR targets on SOI, SiN, and TFLN stacks. A splitter reconstructed from paper passes SOI full-wave simulation. Verifier-guided training improved champion IoU from 0.422 to 0.491 on held-out figures.
AI.conclusion: PixCell establishes a controlled framework for measuring, retargeting, and improving visual-to-parametric photonic component design, demonstrating that frontier multimodal agents can reliably understand and render executable parametric representations from visual targets.

title: DS@GT ARC at MEDIQA-CORE-Task-1 2026: Trimodal Model Fusion with Task-Specific Gates for Brain Tumor Subtype Classification
comment: CLEF 2026 Working Notes, 21 - 24 September 2026, Jena, Germany
summary: Brain tumor diagnosis is a time-sensitive process in which patients may wait weeks for a finalized pathology report. This problem motivates automated systems that classify tumor subtype from multimodal inputs. This paper details the DS@GT ARC team's work for ImageCLEFmed MEDIQA-CORE 2026 Task~1, Brain Tumor Subtype Classification. The task evaluates three glioma classification problems: Level-1 Molecular Type, LGG vs HGG, and WHO Grade. We combine pre-extracted MRI (NeuroVFM) and histopathology (Prov-GigaPath) embeddings with free-text radiology reports. Our team explored two trimodal fusion architectures, two report encoders (RadBERT and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), and a biologically motivated post-processing stage. We achieve a mean macro-F1 of 0.801 under the Fully Multimodal condition, exceeding the organizers' baseline of 0.796 and ranking second among the teams whose code passed verification. Additional evaluation across modality-dropping conditions shows that this advantage depends heavily on the availability of the histopathology modality, and that our system falls behind the baseline when modalities are missing. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/dsgt-arc/imageclef-mediqacore-2026.

AI.tldr: The DS@GT ARC team presents their trimodal (MRI, histopathology, radiology reports) fusion system for ImageCLEFmed MEDIQA-CORE 2026 Task 1 brain tumor subtype classification, achieving mean macro-F1 of 0.801 and ranking second among verified teams, though performance degrades when modalities are missing.
AI.motivation: Brain tumor diagnosis is time-sensitive with patients waiting weeks for pathology reports, motivating automated systems for tumor subtype classification from multimodal inputs to accelerate diagnosis.
AI.method: The team combines pre-extracted embeddings from MRI (NeuroVFM) and histopathology (Prov-GigaPath) with free-text radiology reports. They explore two trimodal fusion architectures, two report encoders (RadBERT and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), and a biologically motivated post-processing stage.
AI.result: Achieved mean macro-F1 of 0.801 under Fully Multimodal condition, exceeding the organizers' baseline of 0.796 and ranking second among verified teams. However, performance falls behind baseline when modalities are missing, with the advantage depending heavily on histopathology availability.
AI.conclusion: Their trimodal fusion approach improves over baseline in the fully multimodal setting, but robustness to missing modalities remains a weakness that should be addressed in future work.

title: DODA: A Database of Datasets for Aesthetics Research
summary: With rapid growth in the fields of empirical and computational aesthetics we have seen a vast increase in large image datasets annotated for aesthetics. As the image databases differ widely in many respects (e.g., different standards for annotation), it can be tedious to find the dataset that fits one's research needs best. The absence of a centralized open-science search system causes additional problems. Currently, researchers typically share dataset links in papers or on diverse platforms like OSF, GitHub or Dropbox. Manually searching for details like image quality and content often requires downloading all datasets. Therefore, we present the Database Of Datasets for Aesthetics (DODA), an intuitive Web application in which researchers can browse all important datasets for aesthetics research. DODA provides general information about these datasets (size, resolution, type of annotation, number of annotators, etc.) and for many of them also precomputed quantitative image properties. We discuss relevant criteria for selecting a suitable dataset with DODA and illustrate the benefits of reusing datasets. Our approach facilitates collaboration across the fields of empirical and computational aesthetics. Keywords: empirical aesthetics, computational aesthetics, machine learning, image annotation, quantitative image properties, Open Science

AI.tldr: The authors present DODA (Database Of Datasets for Aesthetics), a centralized web application that catalogs and provides searchable metadata for image datasets used in aesthetics research, including general information and precomputed quantitative image properties, to help researchers find suitable datasets without manual downloading.
AI.motivation: The rapid growth of empirical and computational aesthetics has led to many disparate image datasets with varying annotation standards, but there is no centralized search system. Researchers must manually download datasets or search across platforms like OSF, GitHub, and Dropbox to find suitable data, which is tedious and inefficient.
AI.method: The authors built DODA, an intuitive web application that catalogs key aesthetics-related image datasets. It provides general metadata (size, resolution, annotation type, number of annotators) and, for many datasets, precomputed quantitative image properties. The paper also discusses criteria for dataset selection and illustrates benefits of dataset reuse.
AI.result: DODA provides a centralized, searchable platform for aesthetics datasets with detailed metadata and precomputed image properties, enabling researchers to compare and select datasets efficiently without downloading all candidates.
AI.conclusion: DODA facilitates cross-disciplinary collaboration between empirical and computational aesthetics by making dataset discovery and comparison easier, supporting Open Science principles.

title: Video Models as Native 4D Renderers: World-Grounded Conditioning from Animated Mesh
summary: Pretrained video diffusion models can act as renderers when the desired scene state is already specified by an animated mesh, a camera trajectory, and a reference image. This 4D generative rendering setting raises a representation question: what image-format condition lets a video backbone obey both camera motion and scene-internal animation? We propose DAR, a reference-guided renderer that extends Wan2.2 camera control from Plücker rays alone to a joint camera-plus-geometry interface. DAR projects a neural 4D G-buffer (tracking, world position, and normal) from the animated mesh and injects it through a widened control adapter while preserving the pretrained image-to-video prior. The central design choice is the pair of tracking and world position. Tracking identifies the persistent surface element that should carry appearance; world position gives its current scene-coordinate state; normal supplies local shape. Depth plus calibrated rays can recover 3D in principle, but depth is a camera-dependent chart in which camera and object motion are mixed. On the 68-case DAR-4D benchmark, LoRA DAR reaches PSNR 23.22, SSIM 0.895, and LPIPS 0.134, improving over off-the-shelf Wan2.2-Depth by 1.54 dB PSNR; a full fine-tune reaches PSNR 25.36 and SSIM 0.917. Matched ablations show that replacing world position by depth reduces PSNR by 1.26--1.55 dB at every checkpoint, supporting tracking+world-position correspondence as a practical 4D rendering condition.

AI.tldr: DAR is a reference-guided 4D generative renderer that extends Wan2.2 camera control by injecting a neural 4D G-buffer (tracking, world position, normal) from an animated mesh through a widened control adapter, achieving state-of-the-art rendering quality over depth-based conditioning.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the representation question of what image-format condition enables a pretrained video diffusion backbone to simultaneously obey both camera motion and scene-internal animation in 4D generative rendering, showing depth is insufficient as it mixes camera and object motion.
AI.method: DAR projects a neural 4D G-buffer containing tracking, world position, and normal attributes from an animated mesh and injects them through a widened control adapter into a pretrained video diffusion model (Wan2.2), extending camera control from Plücker rays to a joint camera-plus-geometry interface.
AI.result: On the 68-case DAR-4D benchmark, LoRA DAR achieves PSNR 23.22, SSIM 0.895, and LPIPS 0.134 (1.54 dB better than Wan2.2-Depth), while full fine-tuning reaches PSNR 25.36 and SSIM 0.917. Ablations show replacing world position with depth reduces PSNR by 1.26-1.55 dB across checkpoints.
AI.conclusion: Tracking plus world-position correspondence serves as a practical and superior 4D rendering condition compared to depth-based alternatives, validating the joint camera-plus-geometry interface design.

title: Logographic Character Visual Pretraining via Semantic-based Contrastive Learning
summary: Current deep learning-based character vision studies, e.g., text recognition, character image denoising, and historical text completion, are offering new solutions for learning, managing, and utilizing character resources. However, the performance of these studies peaks only with large and balanced datasets, which is a rarity with real-world character datasets, especially for logographic character languages, e.g., Chinese. The imbalance in data distribution of logographic characters is a common issue due to differences in character usage frequency and new characters being continuously created. In this paper, we propose a novel method for logographic character recognition, which introduces a multi-modal learning approach using visual semantics and contextual semantics of characters. A novel pre-training strategy is designed to enhance deep visual representations, especially for datasets suffering from issues of imbalanced and rare instances, by extracting the contextual semantics of each character from the corresponding language models. We conduct experiments across various datasets to evaluate our character recognition method and further validate the contrastive pre-training strategy by several downstream tasks. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our method compared to state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a multi-modal learning method for logographic character recognition (e.g., Chinese) that combines visual semantics with contextual semantics extracted from language models, using a novel contrastive pre-training strategy to handle imbalanced and rare character datasets.
AI.motivation: Deep learning-based character vision studies perform well only with large, balanced datasets, but real-world character datasets—especially for logographic languages like Chinese—suffer from data imbalance due to unequal character usage frequency and continuously created new characters. This imbalance limits the performance of existing methods.
AI.method: The paper proposes a multi-modal learning approach that integrates visual semantics with contextual semantics of characters. A novel pre-training strategy is designed to enhance deep visual representations by extracting contextual semantics from language models, specifically targeting datasets with imbalanced and rare instances. Contrastive pre-training is used and validated across multiple downstream tasks.
AI.result: Experimental results across various datasets demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art methods, and the contrastive pre-training strategy is further validated through multiple downstream tasks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed multi-modal approach with contextual-semantic-enhanced contrastive pre-training effectively addresses the data imbalance problem in logographic character recognition and achieves superior performance over existing methods.

title: SPARC-Rad: A Multimodal Benchmark Dataset and Evaluation Pipeline for Spatial and Anatomical Reasoning in Radiology Vision-Language Models
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly being evaluated for medical imaging, but many available benchmarks emphasize disease classification, report generation, or broad visual question answering rather than the spatial and anatomical reasoning required for radiology. We developed the Spatial Perception and Anatomical Reasoning in Clinical Radiology (SPARC-Rad) Benchmark, a manually curated multimodal benchmark dataset and evaluation pipeline for assessing these capabilities in radiology VLMs. SPARC-Rad includes 300 image-question pairs derived from healthy control imaging studies in The Cancer Imaging Archive (TCIA), spanning CT, MRI, and radiography across the abdomen, chest, breast, neuro, and musculoskeletal categories. Radiology trainees manually designed and annotated questions to evaluate anatomical identification, localization, laterality, regional recognition, device identification, and inter-structure spatial relationships. The evaluation pipeline supports standardized prompting, structured output collection, response normalization, LLM-as-judge grading, human quality review, binary correctness scoring, and subgroup analysis by modality, anatomy, and reasoning type. SPARC-Rad provides a reusable framework for evaluating whether VLMs can provide reasoning for radiologic anatomy as a spatial system, supporting future model development, failure-mode analysis, and pre-deployment assessment.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SPARC-Rad, a manually curated multimodal benchmark for evaluating spatial perception and anatomical reasoning capabilities in radiology vision-language models, with 300 image-question pairs across CT, MRI, and radiography modalities.
AI.motivation: Existing VLMs benchmarks for medical imaging focus on disease classification, report generation, or broad visual QA, but neglect the spatial and anatomical reasoning abilities that are essential for radiology practice.
AI.method: SPARC-Rad comprises 300 manually curated image-question pairs derived from healthy control imaging studies in TCIA, spanning CT, MRI, and radiography across abdomen, chest, breast, neuro, and musculoskeletal categories. Questions assess anatomical identification, localization, laterality, regional recognition, device identification, and inter-structure spatial relationships. The evaluation pipeline includes standardized prompting, structured output, response normalization, LLM-as-judge grading, human review, binary scoring, and subgroup analysis by modality, anatomy, and reasoning type.
AI.result: The benchmark provides a reusable evaluation framework for assessing whether VLMs can reason about radiologic anatomy as a spatial system, enabling model development, failure-mode analysis, and pre-deployment assessment.
AI.conclusion: SPARC-Rad addresses a critical gap in medical VLM evaluation by focusing on spatial and anatomical reasoning rather than classification or generation tasks, offering a practical benchmark for validating radiology VLMs before deployment.

title: What Carries the Signal in Pathology Foundation-Model Atlases? A Patient-Level Controlled Benchmark in Breast Cancer
comment: 40 pages, 7 figures, 10 tables. Supplementary Information (16 pages) included as an ancillary file. Segmentation outputs obtained under the Aignostics Research Access Programme; OpenTME data at https://huggingface.co/datasets/Aignostics/OpenTME
summary:
Pathology foundation models are reported to encode molecular programmes in tissue morphology, but the evidence is usually a cohort-wide ranked gene list rather than a prediction for a held-out patient. We rebuild such an analysis with the patient as the unit of evidence and ask which pipeline component carries signal.
  Across 11 frozen backbones, four pre-specified gene programmes and 285 TCGA-BRCA patients with paired slides and RNA-seq (44 cells; GroupKFold by patient, all preprocessing fitted inside the fold), ridge regression on mean-pooled embeddings predicts held-out programme scores at Spearman rho = 0.25-0.56, UNI2 strongest on all four (immune 0.556). A matched permutation null gives raw p ~ 1e-4 at 10,000 permutations for every cell; Holm-adjusted p = 0.0044.
  The signal is real but not uniformly morphological. Against competing models on the same patients and folds, embeddings beat tissue composition for ER/luminal, proliferation and immune (+0.280, +0.284, +0.479; p <= 0.003) but not basal, where compartment fractions alone reach 0.469 against the embedding's 0.493 (p = 0.77). Fifty-four interpretable cell-count features come within 0.043-0.085 on every programme.
  The geometric machinery contributes nothing measurable, and we identify why: the geodesic graph selects neighbours by Euclidean nearest-neighbour search and only reweights edges already chosen, so the topology is Euclidean by construction (Riemannian minus Euclidean = +0.0010, 95% CI [-0.0007, +0.0029]). Applied consistently the geometry is worse (-0.0117). Ridge regression beats the graph-and-metric decoder by +0.097 (CI [+0.069, +0.127]). The driver-count metric common in this literature is near-uninformative here: 91.8% of random six-gene panels recover >=5/6 drivers.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically evaluates whether pathology foundation models can predict molecular programmes from tissue morphology at the patient level, testing 11 frozen backbones on 285 TCGA-BRCA patients with proper cross-validation. While significant signal exists (Spearman rho 0.25-0.56), the study finds the signal is not uniformly morphological across programmes, interpretable cell-count features perform nearly as well, and the Riemannian geometric machinery contributes nothing beyond Euclidean methods (actually performing slightly worse).
AI.motivation: Prior claims that pathology foundation models encode molecular programmes relied on cohort-wide ranked gene lists rather than held-out patient predictions. The authors aim to rigorously test whether these models can actually predict molecular programmes for individual patients and to identify which components of the analysis pipeline carry the predictive signal.
AI.method: Using 11 frozen foundation model backbones, four pre-specified gene programmes, and 285 TCGA-BRCA patients with paired slides and RNA-seq, the authors apply ridge regression on mean-pooled embeddings with GroupKFold by patient (all preprocessing fitted inside the fold). They compare embeddings against tissue composition models and interpretable cell-count features, and dissect the contribution of Riemannian geometric machinery versus standard Euclidean approaches using matched permutation nulls and confidence intervals.
AI.result: UNI2 performs strongest across all four programmes (immune rho=0.556, all rho 0.25-0.56), with significant permutation p-values. Embeddings beat tissue composition for ER/luminal, proliferation and immune programmes but not basal. Interpretable cell-count features come within 0.043-0.085 of embeddings. The geometric machinery contributes nothing measurable (+0.0010), is worse when applied consistently (-0.0117), and ridge regression outperforms graph-and-metric decoders by +0.097. The driver-count metric is near-uninformative (91.8% of random panels recover >=5/6 drivers).
AI.conclusion: The predictive signal from pathology foundation models is real but not uniformly morphological across programmes. Crucially, the Riemannian geometry common in this literature is mathematically redundant—it selects Euclidean nearest neighbours and only reweights existing edges, making it Euclidean by construction. Simple ridge regression and interpretable features are competitive or superior, suggesting that reported geometric advantages may be artifacts of evaluation design rather than genuine modelling gains.

title: Distill What RGB Can Recover: Privileged 3D Evidence for RGB-Only Vision-Language Models
summary: 3D scene understanding requires reasoning about entity existence, spatial layout, and object relations, yet RGB images alone often provide insufficient 3D cues. Existing 3D-VLMs commonly rely on depth or 3D-position-aware inputs at inference time, introducing additional acquisition, reconstruction, or annotation costs that limit RGB-only deployment. We therefore study how training-time 3D evidence can be converted into spatial reasoning capabilities retained under RGB-only inference. We propose a privileged-evidence distillation framework that constructs a distillable teacher through a unified evidence interface and controlled residual injection, and transfers its knowledge to a deployable student receiving only RGB images and questions through logit and structured representation distillation. To avoid imitating teacher signals unsupported by RGB, we further introduce evidence-sensitivity-guided distillation, which uses corrupted evidence to identify highly evidence-dependent targets and down-weight their supervision. We also define a recoverability decomposition based on the matched baseline, teacher, and student, separating privileged gains into RGB-recoverable improvements and residual teacher advantages. Across four benchmarks, the teacher achieves the best result on 7 of 11 reported metrics among the compared methods. The RGB-only student outperforms its matched baseline on all 11 metrics, including gains of 10.4 ScanQA CIDEr and 19.1 Scan2Cap CIDEr@0.5, without additional inference-time inputs. These results validate the effectiveness of training-time privileged 3D evidence distillation for both teacher performance and deployable RGB-only spatial reasoning. Separately, our matched baseline-teacher-student analysis characterizes privileged-gain transfer across evidence types and spatial skills.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a privileged-evidence distillation framework that converts training-time 3D evidence into spatial reasoning capabilities for RGB-only inference. It constructs a distillable teacher using a unified evidence interface and controlled residual injection, then transfers knowledge to an RGB-only student via logit and structured representation distillation, guided by evidence-sensitivity to avoid imitating unsupported signals.
AI.motivation: RGB images alone often provide insufficient 3D cues for scene understanding, but existing 3D-VLMs require depth or 3D-position-aware inputs at inference time, introducing high acquisition, reconstruction, or annotation costs. The authors seek to enable deployable RGB-only spatial reasoning by leveraging 3D evidence at training time only.
AI.method: The framework uses a privileged-evidence distillation approach: (1) a unified evidence interface with controlled residual injection constructs a distillable teacher, (2) knowledge is transferred to an RGB-only student via logit and structured representation distillation, (3) evidence-sensitivity-guided distillation uses corrupted evidence to identify highly evidence-dependent targets and down-weight their supervision, and (4) a recoverability decomposition separates privileged gains into RGB-recoverable improvements and residual teacher advantages.
AI.result: Across four benchmarks, the teacher achieves the best result on 7 of 11 reported metrics. The RGB-only student outperforms its matched baseline on all 11 metrics, including gains of 10.4 ScanQA CIDEr and 19.1 Scan2Cap CIDEr@0.5, without additional inference-time inputs.
AI.conclusion: Training-time privileged 3D evidence distillation effectively improves both teacher performance and deployable RGB-only spatial reasoning. The matched baseline-teacher-student analysis characterizes privileged-gain transfer across evidence types and spatial skills, validating the approach.

title: Counting the Cost of War Under Satellite Embargo: Zero-Shot Estimation of Impacted Infrastructure
summary: Rapid estimation of impacted structures - critical for conflict-zone humanitarian response - is frequently hindered by post-strike satellite data embargoes and imagery blackouts. We bypass this operational bottleneck by reframing impacted building mapping as a zero-shot geometric projection task on archival, pre-strike maps. Using coordinate and incident text from LiveUAMap and ArcGIS, Large Language Models extract weapon payloads (W) to project kinetic blast perimeters via Hopkinson-Cranz scaling (R_base = Z * W^(1/3)). To count exposed structures within these zones without post-strike imagery, we introduce two technical innovations: Adaptive Field-of-View to eliminate resolution (zoom) bias in 2D segmentation (SAMGeo), and 2.5D pseudo-height depth maps combined with segmentation masks to help Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) resolve overlapping, dense rooftops. Evaluated on 2026 Middle East conflict data, depth-augmented LVLMs dramatically outperform traditional segmentation in congested urban centers. This establishes a powerful hybrid paradigm for zero-shot crisis mapping: ultra-fast 2D segmentation for sparse rural zones, and depth-augmented LVLMs for dense urban environments.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a zero-shot crisis mapping framework that estimates impacted structures in conflict zones using archival pre-strike maps instead of post-strike satellite imagery, which is often embargoed. It combines Large Language Models to extract weapon payloads and compute blast perimeters via Hopkinson-Cranz scaling, then uses Adaptive Field-of-View (SAMGeo) for 2D segmentation and 2.5D pseudo-height depth maps with LVLMs for dense urban areas.
AI.motivation: Post-strike satellite data embargoes and imagery blackouts frequently hinder rapid estimation of impacted structures, which is critical for conflict-zone humanitarian response. The paper aims to bypass this operational bottleneck by leveraging archival pre-strike maps instead of relying on unavailable post-strike imagery.
AI.method: The approach reframes impacted building mapping as a zero-shot geometric projection task on archival pre-strike maps. LLMs extract weapon payloads (W) from LiveUAMap and ArcGIS incident text, projecting kinetic blast perimeters via Hopkinson-Cranz scaling (R_base = Z * W^(1/3)). Two technical innovations are introduced: Adaptive Field-of-View to eliminate zoom bias in 2D segmentation (SAMGeo), and 2.5D pseudo-height depth maps combined with segmentation masks to help LVLMs resolve overlapping dense rooftops.
AI.result: Evaluated on 2026 Middle East conflict data, depth-augmented LVLMs dramatically outperform traditional segmentation in congested urban centers, establishing a hybrid paradigm where 2D segmentation excels in sparse rural zones and depth-augmented LVLMs excel in dense urban environments.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a powerful hybrid paradigm for zero-shot crisis mapping, efficiently combining ultra-fast 2D segmentation for sparse areas and depth-augmented LVLMs for dense urban settings, enabling rapid impacted-structure estimation without post-strike imagery.

title: RadPRISM: Schema-stratified radiology-report supervision for concept-disentangled image representations and visual grounding
summary: Vision-language pretraining learns rich medical image representations from radiology reports, but previous model variants commonly operate within a single shared embedding space, so concept-level structure and interpretability must be recovered post hoc, limiting model transparency and, hence, clinical utility. We introduce RadPRISM, which makes a clinician-defined radiology schema a designated stratification axis: an on-premise large language model extracts per-concept text spans from free-text reports, and each clinical concept is aligned in its own dedicated visual subspace, turning concept stratification into direct, top-level alignment supervision. Instantiated on chest radiographs with a 19-concept schema over $203{,}602$ examinations from an internal multi-year archive, RadPRISM improved internal dataset zero-shot classification from $0.717$ (95% CI, $0.710-0.723$) to $0.868$ (95% CI, $0.863-0.872$) macro AUROC over a matched global-alignment baseline, performed on par with the purpose-built CARZero reference in external zero-shot classification while substantially outperforming it (up to 4.3-fold) in pointing-game visual grounding. In addition, a radiologist reader study demonstrated concept-stratified retrieval ability ($0.78$ macro retrieval correctness rate within rank 3), surfacing disentangled descriptive findings that report-level retrieval and fixed-label vocabularies cannot express. RadPRISM yields discriminative, spatially faithful, natively concept-stratified representations shaped by and transparently inspectable by clinicians.

AI.tldr: RadPRISM introduces concept-stratified visual subspaces for medical vision-language pretraining, where each clinical concept from a clinician-defined schema is aligned in its own dedicated embedding space rather than a shared global space, achieving significantly better zero-shot classification, visual grounding, and concept-stratified retrieval on chest radiographs.
AI.motivation: Previous vision-language pretraining models operate in a single shared embedding space, requiring post hoc recovery of concept-level structure and interpretability, which limits model transparency and clinical utility.
AI.method: RadPRISM uses an on-premise large language model to extract per-concept text spans from radiology reports, then aligns each clinical concept in its own dedicated visual subspace, making a clinician-defined radiology schema a direct, top-level alignment supervision axis. It is instantiated on chest radiographs with a 19-concept schema over 203,602 examinations.
AI.result: RadPRISM improved internal dataset zero-shot classification from 0.717 to 0.868 macro AUROC over a matched global-alignment baseline, performed on par with CARZero in external zero-shot classification while substantially outperforming it (up to 4.3-fold) in pointing-game visual grounding. A radiologist reader study showed 0.78 macro retrieval correctness rate within rank 3.
AI.conclusion: RadPRISM yields discriminative, spatially faithful, natively concept-stratified representations that are shaped by and transparently inspectable by clinicians, enabling concept-aware retrieval that fixed-label vocabularies cannot express.

title: SCALP: Semi-Supervised Statistical Shape Modeling from Imperfect 3D Photogrammetry via Landmark-Anchored Spectral Warp
summary: Correspondence-based statistical shape modeling (SSM) is vital for population-level morphometric analysis, but conventional pipelines assume clean, fully registered surfaces. Real-world clinical photogrammetry scans are often noisy, partial, and cluttered, hindering the adoption of radiation-free surface imaging as a safe alternative to computed tomography (CT) for infant craniosynostosis.
