We present SCALP (Semi-supervised Correspondence via lAndmark Localization and sPectral warping), a two-stage framework that constructs consistent shape models directly from raw, imperfect surface scans. First, a semi-supervised Point Transformer leverages a small expert-annotated dataset alongside a large unlabeled cohort to accurately localize craniofacial landmarks with minimal annotation overhead. Second, these landmarks anchor a Laplace--Beltrami spectral deformation of an anatomical template, generating dense correspondences while naturally isolating the cranium from peripheral scanning clutter without manual preprocessing. Experiments on infant photogrammetry scans demonstrate that SCALP consistently outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised point-cloud approaches, offering a clinically practical pathway toward objective, radiation-free head shape analysis.

AI.tldr: SCALP is a two-stage framework for correspondence-based statistical shape modeling that constructs consistent shape models directly from raw, noisy, partial, and cluttered clinical photogrammetry scans. It combines a semi-supervised Point Transformer for craniofacial landmark localization with Laplace-Beltrami spectral warping for dense correspondence generation, enabling radiation-free infant craniosynostosis analysis without manual preprocessing.
AI.motivation: Conventional correspondence-based statistical shape modeling (SSM) pipelines assume clean, fully registered surfaces, but real-world clinical photogrammetry scans are noisy, partial, and cluttered. This limits the adoption of radiation-free surface imaging as a safe alternative to CT for infant craniosynostosis analysis.
AI.method: SCALP consists of two stages: (1) A semi-supervised Point Transformer that leverages a small expert-annotated dataset with a large unlabeled cohort to accurately localize craniofacial landmarks with minimal annotation overhead; (2) These landmarks anchor a Laplace-Beltrami spectral deformation of an anatomical template, generating dense correspondences while naturally isolating the cranium from peripheral scanning clutter without manual preprocessing.
AI.result: Experiments on infant photogrammetry scans demonstrate that SCALP consistently outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised point-cloud approaches for shape modeling from imperfect, raw scans.
AI.conclusion: SCALP offers a clinically practical pathway toward objective, radiation-free head shape analysis for infant craniosynostosis, enabling robust SSM directly from raw clinical scans without manual data cleaning or preprocessing.

title: Manifold-GS: Certified Hybrid Assets via Varifold-Conservative Gaussian Splatting
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) gives high-quality novel-view synthesis, but its adaptive radiance primitives are not directly usable as structured assets: opacity is not an additive area measure, refinement can change the induced geometry, and watertight mesh extraction can hallucinate collision surfaces in unobserved regions. We introduce Manifold-GS, a certified hybrid asset layer for Gaussian scenes. The method separates appearance opacity from geometric quadrature mass, represents surface-like Gaussians as a discrete unoriented varifold, and exports only confidence-certified open surface patches while retaining uncertified content as residual splats. It provides refinement-conservative mass transport, local realizability diagnostics, source-preserving patch bindings, and conservative collision candidates. On three DTU scenes, a frozen asset benchmark shows zero patch-defined edit leakage, texture round-trip PSNR of 30.1/35.3/33.7 dB, and lower collision floater area than official 2DGS meshes on all scenes, with large gaps on two scenes. The result is a precision-coverage tradeoff rather than a universal reconstruction claim. External-region annotations, phantom-collision probes, and 5k-face simplification further support the certified asset interpretation, while RGB-only experiments show that local realizability is not sufficient for sparse-view surface identifiability.

AI.tldr: Manifold-GS introduces a certified hybrid asset layer for 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes, separating appearance opacity from geometric quadrature mass and exporting only confidence-certified open surface patches as assets while retaining uncertified content as residual splats.
AI.motivation: 3D Gaussian Splatting produces high-quality novel-view synthesis but its adaptive radiance primitives cannot be directly used as structured assets due to three key issues: opacity is not an additive area measure, refinement can alter induced geometry, and watertight mesh extraction can hallucinate collision surfaces in unobserved regions.
AI.method: The method separates appearance opacity from geometric quadrature mass, represents surface-like Gaussians as discrete unoriented varifolds, and exports only confidence-certified open surface patches. It provides refinement-conservative mass transport, local realizability diagnostics, source-preserving patch bindings, and conservative collision candidates.
AI.result: On three DTU scenes, the frozen asset benchmark shows zero patch-defined edit leakage, texture round-trip PSNR of 30.1/35.3/33.7 dB, and lower collision floater area than official 2DGS meshes on all scenes with large gaps on two scenes.
AI.conclusion: The approach yields a precision-coverage tradeoff rather than a universal reconstruction claim. External-region annotations, phantom-collision probes, and 5k-face simplification support the certified asset interpretation, while RGB-only experiments show that local realizability alone is insufficient for sparse-view surface identifiability.

title: Learning How Much, Not Just What: Cross-Patient Burden Order for CT Vision-Language Pretraining
summary: Volumetric CT vision-language pretraining learns 3D representations from scan-report pairs, but global and anatomy-aware objectives supervise only correspondence: they establish what is present and leave how much unconstrained. Nothing separates a mild from an extensive case of the same finding along a consistent direction, so the graded burden language in reports collapses into a present/absent signal. Longitudinal supervision would supply this order, but patient-matched CT pairs are scarce at scale; cross-sectional cohorts already encode weak burden cues across different patients. We introduce Spectrum, an anatomy-conditioned framework that represents each study at whole-study and organ scopes. For each organ-mapped pathology, a rule-based scorer mines confidence-filtered lower-to-higher pairs of different patients, and Burden-Direction Alignment (BDA) aligns the pathology-conditioned image delta with the report delta at each scope, separating that direction from its reverse. Because the endpoints are different people, a target-conditioned aligner first makes them comparable, so the delta reflects burden rather than between-patient variation. BDA further separates the selected direction from its reverse, anchors it to the observed higher-burden endpoint, and enforces consistency across ordered triplets. Since every pair is drawn within a single pathology, BDA is designed to constrain intra-class structure that image-report contrast alone never touches. Spectrum attains 85.6 zero-shot AUROC on CT-RATE and 72.7 on external RAD-ChestCT, with consistent gains in linear probing and retrieval. Weak cross-patient order is thus a scalable complement to anatomy-aware correspondence, yielding burden-aware CT representations without longitudinal data.

AI.tldr: Spectrum is an anatomy-conditioned framework that mines cross-patient, confidence-filtered lower-to-higher burden pairs from cross-sectional cohorts and uses Burden-Direction Alignment (BDA) to align pathology-conditioned image deltas with report deltas, yielding burden-aware CT representations without longitudinal data.
AI.motivation: Existing volumetric CT vision-language pretraining uses global and anatomy-aware objectives that only capture what is present (correspondence) but fail to model how much (burden severity). Graded burden language in reports collapses into a present/absent signal, and longitudinal supervision is scarce at scale. Cross-sectional cohorts offer weak burden cues across different patients that remain untapped.
AI.method: Spectrum represents each study at whole-study and organ scopes. A rule-based scorer mines confidence-filtered lower-to-higher burden pairs from different patients for each organ-mapped pathology. Burden-Direction Alignment (BDA) aligns the pathology-conditioned image delta with the report delta at each scope, using a target-conditioned aligner to make cross-patient endpoints comparable. BDA separates the direction from its reverse, anchors to the observed higher-burden endpoint, and enforces consistency across ordered triplets within a single pathology.
AI.result: Spectrum attains 85.6 zero-shot AUROC on CT-RATE and 72.7 on external RAD-ChestCT, with consistent gains in linear probing and retrieval.
AI.conclusion: Weak cross-patient order is a scalable complement to anatomy-aware correspondence, yielding burden-aware CT representations without longitudinal data.

title: Real-Time Visual Obstruction Detection in Surgical Augmented Reality
summary: Surgical augmented reality (AR) can provide contextual guidance by overlaying virtual annotations, tool cues, and procedural information onto the surgical workspace. However, the virtual content may obstruct task-relevant real-world information, such as surgical instruments, and interfere with users' perception during time-sensitive surgical tasks. In this paper, we investigate visual obstruction detection for surgical AR and present a latency-aware pipeline that combines vision-language model (VLM)-based surgical-object recognition with segmentation-based obstruction reasoning. To reduce inference overhead, the system adopts a cascaded small-to-large VLM architecture with segmentation-guided early exiting and attention-based visual token pruning. The small VLM handles easy frames when its key-object prediction is supported by segmentation consistency, while difficult frames are forwarded to a large VLM with pruned visual tokens. We construct a pseudo-AR surgical obstruction detection benchmark by overlaying virtual content onto surgical-tool images and labeling whether the virtual content obstructs task-relevant instruments. Evaluation results show that the proposed system achieves 87.43% obstruction detection accuracy with an average end-to-end latency of 479 ms, reducing latency by 62.90% compared with a cloud large-model baseline. These results demonstrate the feasibility of latency-aware obstruction detection for surgical AR and motivate future work on dynamic surgical videos, multi-object scenes, and clinically grounded AR guidance content.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a latency-aware pipeline for detecting visual obstruction in surgical augmented reality (AR), combining VLM-based surgical-object recognition with segmentation-based obstruction reasoning, using a cascaded small-to-large VLM architecture with segmentation-guided early exiting and attention-based token pruning. The system achieves 87.43% detection accuracy with 479 ms average latency (62.90% reduction vs. cloud baseline).
AI.motivation: Virtual content in surgical AR can obstruct task-relevant real-world information (e.g., surgical instruments), interfering with users' perception during time-sensitive surgical tasks. Existing approaches do not address efficient, real-time obstruction detection.
AI.method: A cascaded small-to-large VLM architecture is proposed. Small VLM handles easy frames when key-object prediction aligns with segmentation consistency; difficult frames are forwarded to a large VLM with attention-based visual token pruning. A pseudo-AR benchmark is constructed by overlaying virtual content onto surgical-tool images with obstruction labels.
AI.result: Achieves 87.43% obstruction detection accuracy with average end-to-end latency of 479 ms, reducing latency by 62.90% compared with a cloud large-model baseline.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate feasibility of latency-aware obstruction detection for surgical AR, motivating future work on dynamic surgical videos, multi-object scenes, and clinically grounded AR guidance content.

title: Attention-Steered Vision-Language Models for Sign Language Translation
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have emerged as a powerful framework for multimodal video understanding. However, they remain limited in the sign language translation task, where we identify a key failure mode of existing VLMbased translators: poor spatial-temporal visual grounding. In particular, we find that standard next-token cross-entropy does not directly provide signal for where and when the model should attend, causing models to overlook sign-relevant regions and frames. To address this challenge, we propose AttnSign, a VLM-based spatial-temporal attention steering framework for sign language translation. AttnSign first introduces spatial attention supervision for sign-relevant regions, such as face and hands, in each frame; then develops an RL-based motion-cadence steering method that encourages the model to explore and focus on sign-level keyframes. Experimental results on How2Sign and OpenASL benchmarks show that our proposed AttnSign consistently outperforms existing methods.

AI.tldr: AttnSign is a VLM-based spatial-temporal attention steering framework for sign language translation that addresses poor visual grounding in existing VLM-based translators by introducing spatial attention supervision on sign-relevant regions (face, hands) and RL-based motion-cadence steering for sign-level keyframe focus, outperforming existing methods on How2Sign and OpenASL benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing VLM-based sign language translators have poor spatial-temporal visual grounding because standard next-token cross-entropy training does not provide explicit signal for where and when the model should attend, causing models to overlook sign-relevant regions and frames.
AI.method: AttnSign introduces (1) spatial attention supervision for sign-relevant regions such as face and hands in each frame, and (2) an RL-based motion-cadence steering method that encourages the model to explore and focus on sign-level keyframes.
AI.result: Experimental results on How2Sign and OpenASL benchmarks show that AttnSign consistently outperforms existing methods.
AI.conclusion: AttnSign effectively addresses the spatial-temporal visual grounding limitation in VLM-based sign language translation by steering attention towards sign-relevant regions and keyframes.

title: Latent-Centroid Steering: Single-Pass Classifier-Free Guidance for Command-Aligned Autonomous Driving
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for end-to-end autonomous driving, enabling agents to map multimodal inputs and high-level navigation instructions directly to executable trajectories. However, in practice, these models exhibit a persistent command-following gap: predicted trajectories often show weak sensitivity to navigation commands, resulting in incorrect behavior at critical decision points. We identify this issue as a form of conditional policy collapse, where regression-based training under multimodal trajectory distributions encourages the model to rely on dominant visual priors while marginalizing the language-conditioned signal. To address this issue, we introduce a principled formulation of classifier-free guidance (CFG) for regression-based vision-language driving. We show that CFG can be interpreted as isolating the instruction-induced residual in the action space by contrasting conditional and unconditional predictions, thereby explicitly amplifying the effect of the navigation command at inference time. However, a standard two-pass CFG introduces prohibitive latency for real-time control and produces noisy instance-level guidance directions. Building on a mean-shift interpretation of CFG, we propose Latent-Centroid Steering (LCS), a single-pass guidance mechanism that replaces instance-level residuals with class-level latent shifts. By projecting conditional representations toward precomputed command-specific centroids, LCS performs class-level latent steering based on cluster geometry that is both more stable and computationally efficient. We demonstrate that LCS reduces inference latency by approximately 50% while achieving stronger command adherence and improved driving performance on both closed-loop (Bench2Drive) and open-loop (nuScenes) benchmarks. Code will be released.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the command-following gap in vision-language driving models by identifying it as conditional policy collapse. The authors introduce Latent-Centroid Steering (LCS), a single-pass classifier-free guidance mechanism that replaces instance-level residual steering with class-level latent shifts toward command-specific centroids, achieving ~50% lower inference latency while improving command adherence and driving performance.
AI.motivation: VLMs for autonomous driving exhibit a persistent command-following gap where predicted trajectories show weak sensitivity to navigation commands. This stems from conditional policy collapse: regression-based training under multimodal trajectory distributions encourages reliance on dominant visual priors while marginalizing language-conditioned signals.
AI.method: The paper formulates classifier-free guidance (CFG) for regression-based vision-language driving, interpreting it as isolating instruction-induced residuals in action space. Building on a mean-shift interpretation, they propose LCS—a single-pass guidance mechanism that replaces noisy, latency-heavy instance-level residuals with stable class-level latent steering by projecting conditional representations toward precomputed command-specific centroids.
AI.result: LCS reduces inference latency by approximately 50% while achieving stronger command adherence and improved driving performance on both closed-loop (Bench2Drive) and open-loop (nuScenes) benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Class-level latent centroid steering in latent space offers a more stable and efficient alternative to instance-level CFG residuals, effectively mitigating conditional policy collapse in vision-language driving while remaining computationally practical for real-time control.

title: Semantically Calibrated Evidence Composition for CT Vision-Language Learning
summary: Learning transferable representations from CT-report pairs requires combining whole-volume context with anatomy-specific evidence. Existing methods typically emphasize either global CT-report alignment or fine-grained anatomy-level correspondence. Global alignment preserves broad study context but leaves the contribution of localized evidence implicit, whereas anatomy-level alignment explicitly grounds local findings but does not specify how independently represented evidence should interact, acquire study-level meaning, and contribute to a global CT representation. To address this gap, we propose SCOPE (Semantic Calibration Of comPosed Evidence), a framework for semantically calibrated evidence composition in CT vision-language learning. Under organ-specific report supervision, mask-guided queries with fixed anatomical identities extract context-aware organ evidence from shared, uncropped volumetric features, while an unrestricted global query retains access to whole-volume context. The global query then drives Local-Global Coupling to compose the organ evidence into a unified evidence representation. The composed evidence is subsequently calibrated using the diagnostic summary, providing study-level semantic supervision beyond local organ descriptions, and is finally integrated as a controlled residual into a context-preserving whole-volume representation aligned with the complete report. This progressive pathway connects localized evidence with study-level semantics without reducing the CT representation to a predefined set of organs. On CT-RATE and RadChestCT, SCOPE achieves macro AUCs of 85.0 and 72.2, respectively, outperforming the previous SOTA by 7.2 and 4.2, while also yielding substantial gains in linear probing and cross-modal retrieval. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of semantically calibrated evidence composition.

AI.tldr: SCOPE is a framework for CT vision-language learning that composes organ-specific evidence into a unified, globally calibrated representation using mask-guided queries, local-global coupling, and diagnostic summary-based semantic calibration.
AI.motivation: Existing CT-report representation learning methods either emphasize global alignment (missing localized evidence) or anatomy-level alignment (lacking a mechanism for how independent evidence interacts and forms global semantics). This gap motivates a method that bridges both.
AI.method: SCOPE uses organ-specific report supervision with mask-guided queries to extract context-aware organ evidence from shared volumetric features, pairs these with a global query via Local-Global Coupling, calibrates the composed evidence using the diagnostic summary, and integrates it as a controlled residual into a context-preserving whole-volume representation aligned with the full report.
AI.result: On CT-RATE and RadChestCT, SCOPE achieves macro AUCs of 85.0 and 72.2, outperforming prior SOTA by 7.2 and 4.2, with substantial gains in linear probing and cross-modal retrieval.
AI.conclusion: Semantically calibrated evidence composition effectively connects localized anatomical evidence with study-level semantics without reducing the CT representation to a fixed set of organs, demonstrating clear improvements over existing approaches.

title: MDWD: A Street-Level Dataset for Municipal Solid Waste Detection in Dense Urban Environments
comment: Accepted for publication at the 14th IEEE European Conference on Visual Information Processing (EUVIP 2026). 6 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables
summary: Automated visual monitoring of urban environments is a growing Computer Vision research area, but municipal solid waste detection remains under-represented in dedicated benchmark resources. Existing waste-related datasets predominantly address individual litter detection, aerial imagery, or image-level classification, and none simultaneously provide street-level imagery, instance-level localization, and categorization of domestic waste streams within a structured municipal collection context. This paper introduces the Maltese Domestic Waste Dataset (MDWD), a street-level benchmark comprising 3,697 high-resolution images and 11,461 manually annotated instances across five domestic waste categories representative of Malta's municipal collection system. The dataset captures substantial variation in location, illumination, object scale, occlusion, and urban context. To establish reproducible baselines, a cross-architecture benchmark is conducted across multiple generations of the YOLO family and a transformer-based detector. On the test set, RF-DETR-M achieves the strongest overall performance with an mAP50 of 94.49% and an F1-score of 93.56%, whilst smaller-capacity variants maintain competitive accuracy at substantially reduced parameter counts. These results indicate that MDWD supports effective training across both compact real-time detectors and transformer-based models, establishing a benchmark for future research in vision-based municipal waste monitoring.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Maltese Domestic Waste Dataset (MDWD), a street-level benchmark with 3,697 high-resolution images and 11,461 annotated instances across five domestic waste categories. The authors benchmark multiple YOLO generations and a transformer-based detector (RF-DETR), with RF-DETR-M achieving the best performance (mAP50 of 94.49%, F1-score of 93.56%), while smaller detectors remain competitive at reduced parameters.
AI.motivation: Municipal solid waste detection is under-represented in benchmark resources. Existing waste datasets only address individual litter detection, aerial imagery, or image-level classification. No dataset simultaneously provides street-level imagery, instance-level localization, and categorization of domestic waste within a structured municipal collection context.
AI.method: The authors construct MDWD, a street-level dataset with 3,697 images and 11,461 manually annotated instances across five domestic waste categories reflecting Malta's municipal collection system. They then conduct a cross-architecture benchmark evaluating multiple YOLO family generations (various parameter counts) and a transformer-based detector (RF-DETR variants).
AI.result: RF-DETR-M achieves the best overall performance with mAP50 of 94.49% and F1-score of 93.56% on the test set. Smaller-capacity YOLO variants maintain competitive accuracy with substantially reduced parameter counts, demonstrating the dataset supports both compact real-time detectors and transformer-based models.
AI.conclusion: MDWD establishes a reproducible benchmark for vision-based municipal waste monitoring, supporting effective training across both lightweight real-time detectors and transformer-based architectures. This fills the gap in street-level domestic waste detection and provides a foundation for future research in this domain.

title: Interpretability-Guided Soft Pruning of Attention Heads in Vision Transformers
summary: Vision foundation models, such as DINOv2, learn highly expressive representations but rely on massive, opaque architectures that demand substantial computational power and memory. To provide an interpretable-guided and efficient solution to this issue, we first propose a spectral analysis and new visualization technique for individual attention heads based on the Laplacian eigenvectors of their attention maps. Building upon recent observations regarding the block structure of Vision Transformers, we perform semantic clustering of attention heads and identify functional redundancies. Leveraging these insights, we introduce SAPER (Soft Attention PrunER), an end-to-end differentiable pruning framework based on the LapSum Soft Top-K approach. Extensive experiments on ImageNet-1K demonstrate that SAPER achieves a highly favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off, outperforming the competitive RAPTOR baseline in FLOPs reduction while preserving strong classification performance.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SAPER, an interpretable-guided pruning framework for Vision Transformers that uses spectral analysis of attention heads, semantic clustering to identify functional redundancies, and a differentiable Soft Top-K pruning approach to achieve efficient model compression with strong accuracy preservation.
AI.motivation: Vision foundation models like DINOv2 achieve excellent representations but are computationally expensive and opaque. The authors aim to provide an interpretable-guided and efficient solution to reduce model size and compute while maintaining performance.
AI.method: The method involves: (1) spectral analysis and novel visualization of attention heads using Laplacian eigenvectors of attention maps, (2) semantic clustering of attention heads to identify functional redundancies, and (3) SAPER, an end-to-end differentiable pruning framework based on the LapSum Soft Top-K approach.
AI.result: Experiments on ImageNet-1K show SAPER achieves a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off, outperforming the RAPTOR baseline in FLOPs reduction while preserving strong classification performance.
AI.conclusion: SAPER demonstrates that interpretability-driven analysis of attention heads can guide effective model pruning, offering a better accuracy-efficiency balance compared to existing pruning methods.

title: ORCA: ORgan-Centroid Aggregation for Training-Free 3D CT Visual Token Compression
summary: A 3D CT scan entering a vision-language model produces a long sequence of visual tokens, often thousands to tens of thousands per volume, and this sequence must be compressed before a language model can consume it. Token compression is well studied in general vision, but little of it targets 3D CT specifically. A common baseline is grid average, which pools regular grid cells and can blend distinct anatomy, lesion, and air into one token. We present \textbf{ORCA} (ORgan-Centroid Aggregation), a token compressor for 3D CT. It merges adjacent tokens with organ guidance and adds a sinusoidal encoding of each region's centroid to preserve spatial layout. This preserves the anatomical information a downstream model needs. ORCA is training-free and plug-and-play, producing an adjustable token set without any model change or text query. We evaluate it across two datasets (CT-RATE and Merlin) and five encoders. The evaluation spans two task types: attribute prediction over five families (size, density, location, texture, and disease) and text generation (visual question answering and report generation). At matched token budgets, ORCA improves consistently over existing compression methods. It shrinks the visual context $64\times$ and its KV-cache $50\times$, and is $31\times$ faster to process each volume. Code released at https://github.com/renjie-liang/ORCA-3DCT.

AI.tldr: ORCA is a training-free, plug-and-play token compressor for 3D CT scans that merges adjacent tokens using organ guidance and sinusoidal centroid encoding, achieving up to 64x context reduction, 50x KV-cache reduction, and 31x speedup while improving downstream performance across attribute prediction and text generation tasks.
AI.motivation: 3D CT scans produce excessively long sequences of visual tokens (thousands to tens of thousands per volume) that must be compressed before entering a vision-language model. Existing token compression methods are designed for general vision and do not target 3D CT specifically; the common grid average baseline pools regular grid cells and can blend distinct anatomy, lesion, and air into a single token, losing critical anatomical information.
AI.method: ORCA (ORgan-Centroid Aggregation) merges adjacent tokens with organ guidance to preserve anatomical information, and adds a sinusoidal encoding of each region's centroid to maintain spatial layout. It is training-free and plug-and-play, requiring no model changes or text queries, and produces an adjustable token set.
AI.result: Evaluated on two datasets (CT-RATE and Merlin) and five encoders, across attribute prediction (size, density, location, texture, disease) and text generation (visual question answering and report generation). At matched token budgets, ORCA consistently outperforms existing compression methods, shrinking visual context 64x, KV-cache 50x, and being 31x faster per volume.
AI.conclusion: ORCA demonstrates that organ-aware token aggregation with spatial encoding substantially outperforms generic compression methods for 3D CT, providing significant efficiency gains while preserving the anatomical information needed by downstream vision-language models.

title: The 1st AI Children Challenge
summary: The First AI Children Challenge aims to advance real-world applications of computer vision and AI in child healthcare, child education, and pediatrics. The 2026 CV4CHL edition featured the first track in this domain: Children Gait Visual Analysis. The main goal of Children Gait Visual Analysis is the fine-grained analysis of children's gait behaviors from keypoint sequences. This is still a big challenge for human action recognition. Experienced medical doctors can distinguish these subtle nuances, but none of the people test AI models in this domain. To bridge this gap, we introduce thousands of 2D children keypoint sequences walking around videos across various age groups of children (3-16 years old). There is a significant opportunity for batch analysis of these videos to provide clinically relevant insights into medical diagnosis. The Challenge will be launched with two problem tracks: Edinburgh Visual Gait Score (EVGS) Scoring and Classification of Gait Patterns in Bilateral Spastic Cerebral Palsy. Each track is chosen in consultation with board-certified pediatricians based on the value of potential solutions. With the first available dataset for such tasks and ground truth for each track, the challenge enabled participants to evaluate their solutions. Final rankings will be revealed after the competition concludes, fostering reproducibility and mitigating overfitting.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the First AI Children Challenge (CV4CHL 2026) focused on Children Gait Visual Analysis, featuring two tracks: Edinburgh Visual Gait Score (EVGS) scoring and classification of gait patterns in bilateral spastic cerebral palsy, using a novel dataset of thousands of 2D keypoint sequences from children aged 3-16.
AI.motivation: Fine-grained gait analysis in children is challenging for AI despite being clinically valuable. Experienced pediatricians can distinguish subtle gait nuances, but no AI models have been developed or tested in this domain. This gap motivates the creation of a benchmark challenge and dataset to advance computer vision applications in child healthcare.
AI.method: The challenge introduces a dataset of thousands of 2D children keypoint sequences from walking videos across ages 3-16. Two problem tracks are launched: (1) Edinburgh Visual Gait Score (EVGS) scoring and (2) classification of gait patterns in bilateral spastic cerebral palsy. Tracks were designed in consultation with board-certified pediatricians based on clinical value.
AI.result: The challenge provides the first available dataset for these tasks with ground truth for each track, enabling participants to evaluate their solutions. Final rankings will be revealed after the competition concludes, fostering reproducibility and mitigating overfitting.
AI.conclusion: This challenge bridges the gap between clinical expertise and AI by providing a benchmark dataset and competition framework for children's gait analysis, with potential to deliver clinically relevant insights for medical diagnosis through batch video analysis.

title: Artificial Intelligence for the Characterization of Particles and Fibers by Optical Microscopy
summary: Optical microscopy of particle and fiber dispersions involves interpreting subtle visual cues influenced by specimen morphology, chemical composition, magnification, and illumination conditions. We introduce an artificial intelligence (AI) distillation framework that extracts semantically rich image embeddings from microscopy images using semantic anchors. A multimodal teacher combines each image's visual embedding with three text embeddings representing illumination modality, magnification, and specimen identity and morphology. Generated by LongCLIP's extended-context text encoder, this yields a 2304-dimensional block-structured teacher vector whose component blocks remain physically interpretable throughout training and inference. A student vision transformer (ViT) with a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) decoder is trained to reconstruct this teacher vector from the image alone, minimizing a mean absolute error (L1) loss that enforces coordinate-level fidelity to the teacher's block structure. A cross-entropy term over pseudo-classes derived from HDBSCAN clustering of the teacher embedding space acts as a collapse-prevention regularizer, enforcing inter-cluster separation without requiring contrastive negative mining. At inference, the student operates on image input alone, producing compact embeddings that recover the full semantic content of the teacher vector. The framework achieves approximately 80% pseudo-class validation accuracy and 75% Recall@1 on fine-grained specimen description labels under leave-one-out nearest-neighbor retrieval. These results demonstrate that semantic anchoring enables a vision-only student to acquire richer and more interpretable representations than image-only training, with direct applicability to retrieval, classification, and exploratory analysis of heterogeneous particle and fiber dispersions.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an AI distillation framework for microscopy images of particle and fiber dispersions, where a multimodal teacher (combining visual and text embeddings from LongCLIP) distills semantically rich, 2304-dimensional block-structured vectors into a vision-only student ViT. The student achieves ~80% pseudo-class validation accuracy and 75% Recall@1 on fine-grained specimen retrieval using only image input.
AI.motivation: Microscopy of particle and fiber dispersions requires interpreting subtle visual cues affected by morphology, composition, magnification, and illumination. Image-only training often fails to capture these semantically rich, multi-modal aspects, motivating a framework that can distill richer representations into a compact vision-only model.
AI.method: A multimodal teacher combines image embeddings with three text embeddings (illumination, magnification, specimen identity/morphology) generated by LongCLIP, producing a 2304-dimensional block-structured teacher vector with physically interpretable components. A student ViT with an MLP decoder is trained to reconstruct this teacher vector from image alone using L1 loss for coordinate-level fidelity, plus a cross-entropy term over HDBSCAN-derived pseudo-classes to prevent representation collapse without contrastive mining.
AI.result: The framework achieves approximately 80% pseudo-class validation accuracy and 75% Recall@1 on fine-grained specimen description labels under leave-one-out nearest-neighbor retrieval, demonstrating that semantic anchoring enables richer and more interpretable representations than image-only training.
AI.conclusion: Semantic anchoring via distillation from a multimodal teacher enables a vision-only student to acquire representations that are richer, more interpretable, and directly applicable to retrieval, classification, and exploratory analysis of heterogeneous particle and fiber dispersions.

title: Decoding Children's Gait Behavior
summary: We introduce a new problem domain for human action recognition: the fine-grained analysis of children's gait behaviors from standard RGB video. We specifically target the ambulatory patterns of children aged 3-17 years. Such behaviors arise naturally in the diagnosis and treatment of several critical developmental and neuromuscular disorders, such as cerebral palsy and hemiplegia. Despite their clinical value, current 3D sensor-based gait analysis systems are expensive, intrusive, and often impractical for young subjects. To address this, we introduce a new dataset comprising over 1,100 high-frame-rate (60 FPS) video sequences from 110 subjects, accompanied by synchronized, anonymized pose sequences. In each session, the child performs a 5-second "walk-around" task, capturing the gait cycle from multiple viewpoints. Crucially, we demonstrate that current state-of-the-art approaches, including gait foundation models and Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), fail to effectively resolve these clinical nuances. We identify the key technical challenges in analyzing these erratic and subtle motor patterns and describe a unified end-to-end framework for decoding fundamental components of pediatric gait. Through comprehensive experimental results, we demonstrate the potential of this dataset to drive novel research questions and establish a rigorous baseline for automated child gait assessment.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a new problem domain—fine-grained child gait analysis from standard RGB video—and presents a new dataset of 1,100+ high-frame-rate video sequences from 110 subjects aged 3-17. The authors show that current SOTA methods (gait foundation models, MLLMs) fail at this task and propose a unified end-to-end framework for decoding pediatric gait, establishing baselines for automated child gait assessment.
AI.motivation: Clinical gait analysis is critical for diagnosing developmental and neuromuscular disorders (e.g., cerebral palsy, hemiplegia) in children, but existing 3D sensor-based systems are expensive, intrusive, and impractical for young subjects. There is a need for accessible, non-intrusive RGB-video-based fine-grained gait analysis.
AI.method: Introduces a new dataset with 1,100+ 60 FPS video sequences from 110 subjects with synchronized pose sequences, where children perform a 5-second walk-around task captured from multiple viewpoints. The paper analyzes failures of existing SOTA methods and describes a unified end-to-end framework for decoding fundamental components of pediatric gait.
AI.result: Shows that current state-of-the-art approaches, including gait foundation models and Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), fail to resolve the clinical nuances of pediatric gait. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the dataset's potential to drive novel research and establish a rigorous baseline for automated child gait assessment.
AI.conclusion: The proposed dataset and framework open a new problem domain in fine-grained child gait analysis from RGB video, addressing the limitations of existing sensor-based systems and establishing a foundation for future automated pediatric gait assessment research.

title: Boosting Generalizable Depth Estimation in Endoscopy by Mixture of Lightweight Experts and Intrinsic Image Alignment
comment: Accepted by MICCAI 2026 @ The Efficient Medical AI (EMA4MICCAI) Workshop (Oral Presentation)
summary: Depth estimation is a significant task for 3D perception in endoscopic surgeries. However, illumination interference and feature diversity in various endoscopic scenes are still challenges for generalizable depth estimation and ego-motion estimation. Based on this, a novel self-supervised framework, EndoMINI, is proposed for depth estimation in endoscopic scenes. Specifically, mixture of low-rank experts (MiLoRE) is proposed to perform parameter-efficient fine-tuning, which can also boost the model adaptation to scenes with different characteristics. Meanwhile, an intrinsic image alignment (IIA) is introduced into the training loss to alleviate the influence of light reflectance in endoscopy with a novel intrinsic image decomposition network. The proposed method is evaluated on SCARED datasets for supervised depth estimation, and two endoscopic datasets, Hamlyn and SERV-CT, for zero-shot depth estimation, compared with state-of-the-art works as well. The experimental results demonstrate outstanding performance of the proposed model and the effects of the main contributions.

AI.tldr: EndoMINI is a novel self-supervised framework for depth estimation in endoscopic scenes, using mixture of low-rank experts (MiLoRE) for parameter-efficient fine-tuning and intrinsic image alignment (IIA) to handle illumination interference. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on SCARED, Hamlyn, and SERV-CT datasets.
AI.motivation: Depth estimation in endoscopic surgeries faces two key challenges: illumination interference and feature diversity across different endoscopic scenes, which hinder generalizable depth and ego-motion estimation.
AI.method: (1) A mixture of low-rank experts (MiLoRE) mechanism for parameter-efficient fine-tuning that adapts the model to scenes with different characteristics. (2) An intrinsic image alignment (IIA) loss with a novel intrinsic image decomposition network to mitigate the influence of light reflectance in endoscopy.
AI.result: Evaluated on SCARED for supervised depth estimation and on Hamlyn and SERV-CT for zero-shot depth estimation, demonstrating outstanding performance compared to state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed EndoMINI framework effectively addresses illumination and scene diversity challenges in endoscopic depth estimation, with experimental results confirming the effectiveness of both MiLoRE and IIA components.

title: Poplar: A Scalable Pipeline for Human-Centric Image Dataset Synthesis
summary: Recent image generators can synthesize convincing human-centric images, yet producing a useful collection remains different from producing a single successful image. A human-centric dataset must cover varied people and contexts, avoid implausible attribute combinations, preserve an everyday photographic character, and expose quality-control decisions at scale. We present Poplar, a reproducible Specify--Render--Inspect pipeline for human-centric image dataset synthesis. Specify samples structured attributes under commonsense constraints and verbalizes them as photography-oriented prompts. Render uses a realism-adapted image generator across composition-aware aspect ratios and retries obvious technical failures. Inspect applies a single structured vision--language review to each candidate, preserving the original prompt while rejecting intrinsic image defects or material prompt mismatches. Using Poplar, we construct Poplar-9K: 9,401 curated human-centric image--text pairs retained from 11,765 reviewed candidates (79.9\% acceptance). We release the dataset together with the pipeline, configurations, immutable generation prompts, and auditable inspection records as a compact resource for building customizable human-centric collections.

AI.tldr: Poplar is a reproducible Specify-Render-Inspect pipeline for synthesizing high-quality human-centric image datasets. It generates structured attributes under commonsense constraints, renders images with a realism-adapted generator, and inspects candidates with vision-language review. The resulting Poplar-9K dataset contains 9,401 curated image-text pairs from 11,765 candidates (79.9% acceptance), released with full pipeline transparency.
AI.motivation: While recent image generators can create convincing single human-centric images, producing a useful dataset collection is fundamentally different from producing a single successful image. A human-centric dataset must cover diverse people and contexts, avoid implausible attribute combinations, maintain everyday photographic character, and expose quality-control decisions at scale—requirements existing approaches do not systematically address.
AI.method: Poplar consists of three stages: (1) Specify—samples structured attributes under commonsense constraints and verbalizes them as photography-oriented prompts; (2) Render—uses a realism-adapted image generator with composition-aware aspect ratios and retries obvious technical failures; (3) Inspect—applies a single structured vision-language review to each candidate, preserving the original prompt while rejecting intrinsic image defects or material prompt mismatches.
AI.result: The pipeline produced Poplar-9K: 9,401 curated human-centric image-text pairs retained from 11,765 reviewed candidates, achieving a 79.9% acceptance rate. The dataset and full pipeline artifacts (configurations, immutable generation prompts, auditable inspection records) are publicly released.
AI.conclusion: Poplar provides a compact, reproducible resource for building customizable human-centric image collections, addressing the gap between generating single successful images and constructing useful datasets at scale with quality control and transparency.

title: Beyond Static Anchors: Bounded Prototype Conditioning for Language-Free Medical Anomaly Detection
summary: Medical anomaly detection identifies abnormal images and localizes lesions under scarce supervision while generalizing across organs and modalities. Existing CLIP-based methods reduce annotation requirements through vision--language alignment, but their normal and abnormal references, whether text prompts or learned visual tokens, remain fixed across test images. Such static references may not transfer reliably to unseen targets in a cross-domain medical imaging scenario. To address this, we propose ReCAP, a language-free framework that replaces static anchors with input-conditioned visual prototypes. ReCAP re-centers separated normal and abnormal prototypes for each image through a bounded gated modulation, enabling query-adaptive anomaly scoring while constraining context-induced prototype drift. For the few-shot setting, we introduce a non-parametric normal-reference memory to preserve instance-level target-domain variation and complement the conditional prototype branch. Across six medical benchmarks, ReCAP achieves the best image-level AUROC on all zero-shot and 23 of 24 few-shot settings, and the best zero-shot pixel-level AUROC on all three segmentation datasets. Particularly, it reduces inference latency by over 70% compared to the fastest baseline, without text prompts or test-time gradient updates.

AI.tldr: ReCAP is a language-free framework for medical anomaly detection that replaces static CLIP-based references (text prompts or learned visual tokens) with input-conditioned visual prototypes, achieving state-of-the-art performance across six medical benchmarks with over 70% faster inference.
AI.motivation: Existing CLIP-based medical anomaly detection methods use static normal/abnormal references that remain fixed across test images, which fail to transfer reliably to unseen targets in cross-domain medical imaging scenarios.
AI.method: ReCAP replaces static anchors with input-conditioned visual prototypes by re-centering separated normal and abnormal prototypes per image via bounded gated modulation. For few-shot settings, it adds a non-parametric normal-reference memory to preserve instance-level target-domain variation and complement the conditional prototype branch.
AI.result: ReCAP achieves the best image-level AUROC on all zero-shot and 23 of 24 few-shot settings, and best zero-shot pixel-level AUROC on all three segmentation datasets. It reduces inference latency by over 70% compared to the fastest baseline without text prompts or test-time gradient updates.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, input-conditioned prototypes are more effective than static references for cross-domain medical anomaly detection, offering both better accuracy and significantly lower computational cost.

title: Reconstruction-Shift Discrimination via Mask-Guided Latent Diffusion for Medical Anomaly Detection
summary: Unsupervised medical anomaly detection learns normal anatomical patterns from healthy training images and identifies deviations at test time. Reconstruction-based and diffusion-based methods commonly use the difference between an input image and its reconstruction as anomaly evidence. However, this residual can be ambiguous. Expressive models may preserve pathological structures, while benign anatomical variation, imaging noise, and acquisition differences may also produce large reconstruction errors. We propose discriminative mask-guided diffusion (DMD), a medical anomaly detection framework that complements residual-based localization with reconstruction-shift discrimination. DMD first learns a compact quantized latent representation of normal images. Localized masks then perturb selected latent regions, and a latent diffusion model reconstructs the perturbed representations. The resulting reconstructions are paired with their original normal images to define a self-supervised classification task. At inference, the classifier provides a learned image-level anomaly score, while the residual between the input and its diffusion-based reconstruction yields a pixel-level anomaly map. Experiments on five datasets spanning brain MRI, breast ultrasound, and chest radiography show that DMD achieves the best overall performance among the state-of-the-art baseline methods.

AI.tldr: DMD is a medical anomaly detection framework that combines residual-based localization (via diffusion reconstruction) with a learned reconstruction-shift discrimination classifier, achieving state-of-the-art performance across five medical imaging datasets.
AI.motivation: Traditional reconstruction/diffusion-based anomaly detection uses input-reconstruction residuals as anomaly evidence, but these residuals are ambiguous—expressive models may preserve pathologies while benign variation and noise can produce large errors. A more discriminative approach is needed.
AI.method: DMD first learns a compact quantized latent representation of normal images. It then applies localized masks to perturb selected latent regions, and a latent diffusion model reconstructs the perturbed representations. Reconstructions are paired with original normal images to define a self-supervised classification task. At inference, the classifier provides a learned image-level anomaly score, while the residual between input and diffusion reconstruction yields a pixel-level anomaly map.
AI.result: Experiments on five datasets spanning brain MRI, breast ultrasound, and chest radiography show that DMD achieves the best overall performance among state-of-the-art baseline methods.
AI.conclusion: Complementing residual-based anomaly localization with learned reconstruction-shift discrimination improves medical anomaly detection accuracy, addressing the ambiguity of reconstruction residuals.

title: Structured Proxy Features for Multimodal NSCLC Survival Prediction from Pretreatment CT
summary: Lung cancer results in roughly 1.8 million fatalities annually worldwide, with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) comprising the majority of cases. Despite advancements in treatment, survival stratification remains challenging due to intratumoral heterogeneity inadequately captured by conventional descriptors. Standard radiomic and deep learning techniques regard imaging features as independent quantities, overlooking structured interactions between tumor characteristics. We evaluate whether structured proxy features can enhance multimodal NSCLC survival prediction by augmenting pretreatment computed tomography (CT) representations, radiomics, and clinical variables with six simulation-derived features designed to capture interactions between heterogeneity and morphology. A radiomic-parameterized cellular automaton generates growth-rate and necrosis-ratio proxy features from baseline CT by using entropy and sphericity to compute low-dimensional proxy parameters. The imaging backbone is a Transformer-based Masked Autoencoder (TMAE), which was chosen after a systematic evaluation with alternative encoders within the same pipeline and provides attention-based visualizations that highlight tumor regions receiving higher model attention. On the public Lung1 cohort (n = 390), the primary four-modality fusion attained a C-index of 0.641 (iAUC 0.731, log-rank p < 0.001). The primary result compares favorably with prior multimodal results on Lung1 (C-index 0.631; iAUC 0.592 [15]) under a comparable evaluation protocol, while a separate exploratory coefficient-optimization analysis achieved a best observed C-index of 0.662 (iAUC 0.748). These results indicate that, in addition to conventional radiomic, deep, and clinical representations within the Lung1 benchmark, simulation-derived proxy features may provide complementary predictive information within this fixed Lung1 benchmark.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates whether simulation-derived proxy features can enhance multimodal NSCLC survival prediction by augmenting CT representations, radiomics, and clinical variables with six features capturing interactions between heterogeneity and morphology. Using a Transformer-based Masked Autoencoder backbone on the Lung1 cohort, the four-modality fusion achieved C-index 0.641, outperforming prior multimodal results.
AI.motivation: Survival stratification for NSCLC remains challenging due to intratumoral heterogeneity not captured by conventional descriptors. Standard radiomic and deep learning techniques treat imaging features as independent quantities, overlooking structured interactions between tumor characteristics.
AI.method: A radiomic-parameterized cellular automaton generates growth-rate and necrosis-ratio proxy features from baseline CT using entropy and sphericity. The imaging backbone is a Transformer-based Masked Autoencoder (TMAE), selected after systematic comparison with alternative encoders. These proxy features augment CT representations, radiomics, and clinical variables for multimodal fusion.
AI.result: On the Lung1 cohort (n=390), the primary four-modality fusion achieved C-index 0.641 (iAUC 0.731, log-rank p<0.001), comparing favorably to prior multimodal results (C-index 0.631; iAUC 0.592). An exploratory coefficient-optimization analysis achieved best observed C-index 0.662 (iAUC 0.748).
AI.conclusion: Simulation-derived proxy features may provide complementary predictive information beyond conventional radiomic, deep, and clinical representations for NSCLC survival prediction within the Lung1 benchmark.

title: Scene2Sound: Auditory-Grounded Soundscape Generation for 3D Gaussian Worlds
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) turns captured or generated imagery into photorealistic 3D world simulations that users can freely explore, yet these worlds remain silent. Because existing audio generation methods condition on a single image or viewpoint, their sound is tied to that observation and cannot stay consistent while a listener moves. We introduce the task of generating a spatially consistent soundscape for a given 3DGS world through auditory grounding, identifying which objects in the world should emit sound and anchoring each to a persistent 3D position, and present Scene2Sound, a training-free framework built on this grounding. From the input world alone, our pipeline selects viewpoints that jointly cover the scene, identifies sound-emitting objects with a vision-language model, and associates the multi-view detections into 3D instances through Gaussian set matching, which measures the overlap between the Gaussian sets that render each detection. Each source then receives generated audio that a standard object-based audio engine spatializes in real time at arbitrary listener poses. We further propose two spatial-consistency metrics, one testing whether rendered audio responds consistently to listener motion and one testing whether the claimed sources are supported by views held out from their placement. On a curated set of generated 3DGS worlds and on 3DGS scenes generated from real-world 360-degree captures, Scene2Sound preserves the audio quality of strong per-viewpoint baselines while remaining spatially consistent where per-viewpoint and single-panorama pipelines do not, and a user study confirms the perceptual benefit. Project page: https://masaki-lmd.github.io/scene2sound/.

AI.tldr: Scene2Sound is a training-free framework that generates spatially consistent soundscapes for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) worlds. It identifies sound-emitting objects via multi-view detection and vision-language models, anchors them to persistent 3D positions through Gaussian set matching, and spatializes generated audio in real time. It introduces two spatial-consistency metrics and demonstrates improved consistency over per-viewpoint baselines.
AI.motivation: 3DGS recreates photorealistic 3D worlds but they remain silent. Existing audio generation methods condition on a single image or viewpoint, so sound is tied to that observation and breaks consistency as the listener moves. There is a need for generating soundscapes that remain spatially coherent across arbitrary listener poses in 3D worlds.
AI.method: Scene2Sound is a training-free pipeline built on auditory grounding. It selects viewpoints covering the scene, identifies sound-emitting objects using a vision-language model, and associates multi-view detections into 3D instances via Gaussian set matching (measuring overlap between Gaussian sets rendering each detection). Each source gets generated audio spatialized by an object-based audio engine at arbitrary listener poses. Two spatial-consistency metrics are proposed.
AI.result: On curated generated 3DGS worlds and 3DGS scenes from real 360-degree captures, Scene2Sound preserves audio quality comparable to strong per-viewpoint baselines while remaining spatially consistent where per-viewpoint and single-panorama pipelines fail. A user study confirms the perceptual benefit.
AI.conclusion: Auditory grounding through 3D instance association enables training-free, spatially consistent soundscape generation for 3DGS worlds, addressing a gap in existing audio generation methods that tie sound to single viewpoints.

title: CrossProjection: Geometric Grounding Beyond Viewpoint Change in Architectural Drawings
comment: Initial controlled diagnostic study on 23 natural drawing sets and three VLMs; broader model, building, repeated-inference, and human coverage is planned for a subsequent version
summary:
Architectural drawings violate the usual assumption behind multi-view reasoning: plans and sections are cuts, while elevations are facade projections, so corresponding components change appearance in ways camera motion cannot explain. We introduce CrossProjection, an anchor-grounded diagnostic of whether vision-language models preserve component identity and externalize geometry across heterogeneous architectural views. It evaluates Matching, Registration, and Geometric Grounding through categorical judgments, candidate selection, and free point, line, and region localization.
  Across 23 real drawing sets and 1,954 categorical conditions per model, GPT-5.5 scores 82.4%, Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct 62.2%, and GLM-4.5V 57.2%. A matched 200-target study crosses natural and vector-text-suppressed drawings with closed-candidate and free-geometry outputs. Candidate-supported performance is often higher, but free localization remains fragile: on natural drawings, point/region PCK@.05 is 54-76% for GPT, 8-10% for Qwen, and 14-36% for GLM; line endpoint PCK@.05 is 22%, 4%, and 0%. A coordinate grid recovers some GPT point/region precision but not lines. Three architecture-trained participants reach 87.3-93.3% categorical accuracy and 76-92% GT-region hit, supporting task feasibility rather than a population-level human ceiling.
  Because the categorical families do not form a same-item Matching-Registration contrast and interface controls alter multiple burdens, we avoid mechanistic claims. The supported conclusion is narrower: closed-choice or marked-element success does not entail reliable explicit geometric grounding. For drawing-guided CAD/BIM systems, categorical correctness should not be treated as evidence of candidate-free spatial reliability. Reusable on-sheet anchors, fixed-denominator scoring, and hash-locked artifacts establish an audit trail for this gap.

AI.tldr: CrossProjection is a benchmark diagnosing whether vision-language models preserve component identity and externalize geometry across heterogeneous architectural view types (plans, sections, elevations), finding that categorical accuracy does not entail reliable free-geometry localization.
AI.motivation: Architectural drawings break the standard multi-view assumption: plans/sections are cuts while elevations are projections, so the same component changes appearance in ways camera motion cannot explain. Existing evaluations cannot test whether VLMs truly preserve identity and geometry across such heterogeneous views.
AI.method: CrossProjection evaluates models on Matching, Registration, and Geometric Grounding via categorical judgments, candidate selection, and free point/line/region localization. Tested across 23 real drawing sets with 1,954 categorical conditions per model, including natural and vector-text-suppressed drawings, closed-candidate and free-geometry outputs, and a coordinate-grid augmentation.
AI.result: GPT-5.5 scores 82.4%, Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct 62.2%, GLM-4.5V 57.2% on categorical conditions. Free localization is fragile: point/region PCK@.05 is 54-76% (GPT), 8-10% (Qwen), 14-36% (GLM); line endpoint PCK@.05 is 22%, 4%, 0%. Coordinate grids help GPT on points/regions but not lines. Three architecture experts reach 87.3-93.3% categorical and 76-92% GT-region hit rates.
AI.conclusion: Closed-choice or marked-element success does not imply reliable explicit geometric grounding. For CAD/BIM drawing-guided systems, categorical correctness should not be treated as evidence of candidate-free spatial reliability. The benchmark provides an audit trail via reusable anchors, fixed-denominator scoring, and hash-locked artifacts.

title: DreamTraj: Generating 6-DoF Object Trajectories by Reading Unrendered Video Diffusion Latents
comment: 17 pages, 8 figures, 11 tables. Project page: https://whathappen0.github.io/DreamTraj/
summary: Accurate prediction of object trajectories during manipulation is essential for closing the perception-action loop. Progress is limited on two fronts: available datasets lack fine-grained language-to-motion annotations, and existing predictors either rely on privileged inputs such as video, depth, or CAD models, or recover motion from fully generated videos through costly, error-prone perception pipelines. We close the supervision gap with the MOVE dataset, 5,038 object-centric egocentric trajectories, each paired with a fine-grained natural-language instruction rather than a coarse verb-noun label. We further propose DreamTraj, which predicts a 6-DoF object trajectory from a single RGB image and a task instruction, requiring no video, depth, or CAD model at inference: rather than generating a video, it reads motion from the internal representations of a frozen image-to-video diffusion model at an early denoising step. A lightweight flow-matching Reader decodes query-key attention tracks and pooled hidden states into relative 6-DoF poses. To our knowledge, this is the first approach to directly decode object 6-DoF trajectories from intermediate video diffusion representations rather than generated pixels. DreamTraj sets a new state of the art on both translation and rotation against forecasters that consume multi-frame or privileged inputs, and runs 4.6x faster than generate-then-extract pipelines.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the MOVE dataset (5,038 object-centric egocentric trajectories with fine-grained natural-language instructions) and DreamTraj, a method that predicts 6-DoF object trajectories from a single RGB image and task instruction by decoding intermediate representations of a frozen image-to-video diffusion model, achieving state-of-the-art results while running 4.6x faster than generate-then-extract pipelines.
AI.motivation: Object trajectory prediction during manipulation is essential for closing the perception-action loop, but progress is limited by (1) datasets lacking fine-grained language-to-motion annotations and (2) existing predictors relying on privileged inputs (video, depth, CAD models) or costly error-prone perception pipelines over generated videos.
AI.method: DreamTraj uses a frozen image-to-video diffusion model and reads motion from its internal representations at an early denoising step rather than generating a video. A lightweight flow-matching Reader decodes query-key attention tracks and pooled hidden states into relative 6-DoF poses.
AI.result: DreamTraj sets a new state of the art on both translation and rotation against forecasters that consume multi-frame or privileged inputs, and runs 4.6x faster than generate-then-extract pipelines.
AI.conclusion: This is the first approach to directly decode object 6-DoF trajectories from intermediate video diffusion representations rather than generated pixels, demonstrating an efficient and accurate alternative to video-generation-based trajectory prediction.

title: Practical Noise Modeling for SPAD Intensity Imaging
summary: Single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) cameras are promising for low-light and high-dynamic-range intensity imaging, but their practical use is limited by complex sensor-specific noise. Unlike time-correlated single-photon counting (TCSPC) systems, SPAD cameras record whether at least one detection occurred in each gate without photon timestamps in intensity imaging mode, making explicit noise decomposition difficult. We present a practical noise modeling and calibration framework for SPAD intensity denoising. Our forward model describes binary-frame accumulation with a Binomial observation process, models signal-independent dark noise as an exposure-dependent pure dark count term plus an exposure-independent dark-frame bias term, and incorporates pixel-wise response non-uniformity. We design a dedicated calibration procedure for the proposed model and use it to build a count-domain noise-synthesis pipeline for network training. For denoising, we further design a SPAD-specific dark-shading correction (SPAD-DSC) to remove most systematic noise before network training. We construct a real-world SPAD intensity dataset for testing. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed noise model.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a practical noise modeling and calibration framework for SPAD camera intensity denoising, using a Binomial forward model with explicit dark noise decomposition and pixel-wise non-uniformity correction.
AI.motivation: SPAD cameras are promising for low-light and HDR imaging but are limited by complex sensor-specific noise. Unlike TCSPC systems, SPAD cameras in intensity mode record only binary frame events without photon timestamps, making explicit noise decomposition difficult.
AI.method: The framework models binary-frame accumulation as a Binomial observation process, decomposes dark noise into an exposure-dependent pure dark count term plus an exposure-independent dark-frame bias, incorporates pixel-wise response non-uniformity, and designs a dedicated calibration procedure with a count-domain noise-synthesis pipeline for network training, along with a SPAD-specific dark-shading correction (SPAD-DSC).
AI.result: A real-world SPAD intensity dataset was constructed for testing, and experimental results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed noise model.
AI.conclusion: The proposed noise modeling and calibration framework effectively addresses SPAD-specific noise challenges, improving intensity denoising performance.

title: Image-Space Rule Discovery
summary: Can image-editing models discover visual rules in image space and complete problem-solving end-to-end? We tackle this question in the spirit of a human worksheet test (e.g., an IQ test), using problems that require models to read image-based instructions, recognize the problem, infer the answer, bind it to the correct destination, control output count, suppress unnecessary edits, and preserve the input and format. We introduce WISRD, a Worksheet Image-Space Rule Discovery benchmark with 11 core tasks under eight information conditions, spanning localized marking, filling, copying, counting, and no-edit suppression, together with four supplementary reasoning-stress probes for multi-step spatial manipulation, abstract pattern reasoning, logical inference, and constraint-based problem solving. We identify three key findings as follows. (i) Among the frontier image-editing models evaluated, Nano Banana Pro achieves the highest score. On the shared V0--V3 no-reference subset, the Auto-Strict proxy pass rates are 48.7% for Nano Banana Pro, 13.4\% for Qwen-Image-Edit, 11.5% for FLUX.2 Klein 4B API, 11.3% for FLUX.2 Klein 4B open-weight, and 0.0% for InstructPix2Pix. (ii) Analysis reveals that current image-editing models can partially rely on rendered in-image instructions even when the external prompt is absent or merely generic. (iii) In small supplementary diagnostics, Nano Banana Pro achieves 70.0% on 4-by-4 Sudoku and 22.9% on public RAVEN pattern-discovery items in image space.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces WISRD, a benchmark for testing whether image-editing models can discover visual rules in image space and solve problems end-to-end, finding that current models (led by Nano Banana Pro) can partially perform such reasoning but with significant limitations.
AI.motivation: The authors ask whether image-editing models can go beyond editing to actually perform visual rule discovery and problem-solving directly in image space, akin to human IQ tests. This probes a fundamental capability question about whether image-editing models can serve as end-to-end visual reasoning systems.
AI.method: The paper presents WISRD, a benchmark with 11 core tasks across 8 information conditions (localized marking, filling, copying, counting, no-edit suppression) plus 4 reasoning-stress probes (multi-step spatial manipulation, abstract pattern reasoning, logical inference, constraint-based problem solving). Multiple frontier image-editing models are evaluated, including Nano Banana Pro, Qwen-Image-Edit, FLUX.2 Klein 4B, and InstructPix2Pix.
AI.result: Nano Banana Pro achieves the highest performance (48.7% on the Auto-Strict proxy pass rate), far surpassing other models (13.4% for Qwen-Image-Edit, ~11% for FLUX.2 variants, 0% for InstructPix2Pix). Models can partially rely on rendered in-image instructions even without external prompts. Nano Banana Pro reaches 70.0% on 4x4 Sudoku and 22.9% on RAVEN pattern items.
AI.conclusion: Current image-editing models show emerging but limited capabilities for end-to-end visual rule discovery and reasoning in image space. The large performance gap between the best model and others, combined with the still-moderate absolute scores, indicates substantial room for improvement in this direction.

title: Optical Flow from Photons
summary: Optical flow remains challenging in high-speed and low-light scenes, where the limited frame rate and sensitivity of conventional cameras lead to motion blur and underexposure. Single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) cameras offer single-photon sensitivity and extremely fine temporal sampling. However, individual slices in these high FPS binary photon streams are too sparse for dense correspondence. Temporal aggregation can provide the spatial cues required by optical flow, but accumulating photons at fixed coordinates blurs moving structures. Motion-aware aggregation can reduce this blur, yet it depends on the flow being estimated. To address this dependency, we propose QuantaFlow, the first method for dense optical flow directly from SPAD streams. Instead of constructing a fixed input representation, QuantaFlow embeds SPAD representation construction into iterative flow refinement. At each iteration, the current flow coarsely aligns the slices within the source and target sub-streams. A photon-flux transformation then constructs multi-scale representations containing intensity and structural cues, while adaptive multi-scale fusion balances photon noise and residual motion blur at each pixel. The fused representations drive a feature-warping flow update, and the refined flow guides representation construction in the next iteration. We further construct a synthetic dataset for SPAD optical-flow training and evaluation. Experiments on the synthetic dataset and real-world SPAD data demonstrate the effectiveness and generalization of QuantaFlow.

AI.tldr: QuantaFlow is the first method for dense optical flow directly from single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) camera streams. It embeds SPAD representation construction into iterative flow refinement, using current flow estimates to align slices and construct multi-scale representations that balance photon noise and motion blur, achieving robust performance in high-speed and low-light scenes.
AI.motivation: Optical flow estimation in high-speed and low-light scenes is challenging due to motion blur and underexposure from conventional cameras. While SPAD cameras offer single-photon sensitivity and fine temporal sampling, individual binary photon slices are too sparse for dense correspondence, and naive temporal aggregation blurs moving structures. Motion-aware aggregation helps but depends on the flow being estimated, creating a chicken-and-egg problem.
AI.method: QuantaFlow embeds SPAD representation construction into an iterative flow refinement loop. At each iteration: (1) current flow coarsely aligns slices in source and target sub-streams, (2) a photon-flux transformation builds multi-scale representations capturing intensity and structure, (3) adaptive multi-scale fusion balances photon noise and residual motion blur per pixel, and (4) fused representations drive a feature-warping flow update that refines the flow for the next iteration. A synthetic dataset is also constructed for training and evaluation.
AI.result: Experiments on both the synthetic dataset and real-world SPAD data demonstrate the effectiveness and generalization of QuantaFlow for dense optical flow estimation from SPAD streams.
AI.conclusion: QuantaFlow shows that jointly optimizing representation construction and flow estimation in a closed loop can overcome the sparsity and blur challenges of SPAD-based optical flow, providing a viable solution for extreme imaging conditions.

title: SpatialAfford: Teaching Compact VLMs Where to Look and Where to Ground for Affordance
summary: Affordance grounding aims to localize the functional region for interaction, such as the handle to grasp or the button to press, rather than the whole object. This makes it more challenging than generic visual grounding because the target region is smaller, more ambiguous, and more dependent on task context, especially for compact vision-language models (VLMs) used in embodied settings. Recent sequence-level supervision and reinforcement learning improve coordinate prediction quality, yet compact autoregressive VLMs still lack reliable affordance-aware visual focus before coordinate generation: the model can produce better coordinate tokens while its cross-modal attention remains diffuse and weakly anchored to the true affordance evidence. To address it, we propose SpatialAfford, a two-stage framework that first aligns attention to the ground-truth affordance region through Spatial Attention Alignment (SAA), then refines coordinate prediction with Spatial-Aware GRPO. By explicitly teaching the model where to look before optimizing where to ground, SpatialAfford turns affordance grounding from a purely output-constrained objective into attention-grounded spatial reasoning. Across ShareRobot-Bench, ReasonAff, and PartAfford, SpatialAfford consistently improves affordance grounding, with a compact 4B model outperforming stronger 7B+ baselines.

AI.tldr: SpatialAfford is a two-stage framework that improves affordance grounding in compact VLMs by first aligning cross-modal attention to ground-truth affordance regions via Spatial Attention Alignment (SAA), then refining coordinate prediction with Spatial-Aware GRPO. A compact 4B model using this approach outperforms stronger 7B+ baselines across ShareRobot-Bench, ReasonAff, and PartAfford.
AI.motivation: Compact autoregressive VLMs in embodied settings fail to achieve reliable affordance-aware visual focus before generating coordinates—their cross-modal attention remains diffuse and weakly anchored to true affordance evidence, even when coordinate tokens improve under sequence-level supervision or RL. This gap between output quality and attention grounding motivates the need to explicitly teach the model where to look.
AI.method: A two-stage framework: (1) Spatial Attention Alignment (SAA) which aligns model attention to the ground-truth affordance region, and (2) Spatial-Aware GRPO which refines coordinate prediction using spatial-aware reinforcement learning. The framework explicitly teaches the model where to look before optimizing where to ground.
AI.result: SpatialAfford consistently improves affordance grounding across ShareRobot-Bench, ReasonAff, and PartAfford benchmarks. A compact 4B model outperforms stronger 7B+ baselines.
