AI.method: The pipeline preserves real spherical coordinates from geometric mapping throughout all stages, uses a lightweight enhancement module with frequency-domain supervision to bridge the event-image domain gap, and employs a spherical Transformer with 3D positional embeddings for photometric reconstruction in an end-to-end learnable framework.
AI.result: On synthetic data and captured rotational scans, E2Pano achieves improved reconstruction quality and lower photometric reconstruction cost than optimization-based baselines. It also shows encouraging transfer to real captures under their acquisition protocol despite being trained purely on synthetic data.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that a geometry-guided, end-to-end learnable approach can effectively reconstruct panoramic images from event streams, and provides the PanoScan dataset to support further research in this direction.

title: FreqAnchorAD: Language-Free Zero-Shot Anomaly Detection via Frequency-Deviation Anchoring
summary: Zero-shot anomaly detection (ZSAD) aims to detect anomalies and localize defective regions in unseen target domains without target training data. Recent ZSAD methods build on pretrained vision models, particularly CLIP, and construct normal and anomaly references from textual prompts or learnable visual representations. These methods perform anomaly discrimination primarily in spatial feature spaces, where subtle changes in texture, boundaries, and local structures can be confused with normal appearance variations. Although inconspicuous spatially, such defects can disrupt local texture regularity or boundary continuity, inducing response deviations across frequency bands. However, existing ZSAD methods do not explicitly model these frequency-dependent characteristics. Our image-domain analysis reveals that local defects exhibit spatial-frequency deviations from normal references across low-, middle-, and high-frequency bands, indicating that anomaly evidence is not universally dominated by high-frequency responses. Motivated by this observation, we propose FreqAnchorAD, a frequency-aware framework that organizes frequency-enhanced responses for anchor-relative anomaly discrimination. Specifically, the Local Frequency Compensation Module (LFCM) enhances intermediate patch tokens with local spatial-frequency cues. The Frequency-Deviation Anchor Projector (FDAP), our core discrimination module, organizes enhanced responses along a source-derived channel coordinate and measures anomaly evidence through relative similarity to normal and anomaly anchors. Finally, Asymmetric Anchor Supervision (AAS) stabilizes normal-anchor alignment while preserving diverse anomaly patterns. Experiments on thirteen industrial and medical benchmarks show that FreqAnchorAD achieves state-of-the-art mean performance in image-level anomaly recognition and pixel-level defect localization.

AI.tldr: FreqAnchorAD is a frequency-aware zero-shot anomaly detection framework that leverages spatial-frequency deviations across low-, mid-, and high-frequency bands to improve anomaly recognition and defect localization in unseen target domains, achieving SOTA results on thirteen industrial and medical benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing ZSAD methods operate primarily in spatial feature spaces and fail to explicitly model frequency-dependent characteristics of defects. The authors show through image-domain analysis that local defects exhibit frequency deviations across all bands (not just high-frequency), motivating the need for explicit frequency modeling in anomaly detection.
AI.method: FreqAnchorAD consists of three key components: (1) Local Frequency Compensation Module (LFCM) enhances intermediate patch tokens with local spatial-frequency cues; (2) Frequency-Deviation Anchor Projector (FDAP) organizes enhanced responses along a source-derived channel coordinate and measures anomaly evidence via relative similarity to normal and anomaly anchors; (3) Asymmetric Anchor Supervision (AAS) stabilizes normal-anchor alignment while preserving diverse anomaly patterns.
AI.result: Experiments on thirteen industrial and medical benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art mean performance in both image-level anomaly recognition and pixel-level defect localization.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that anomaly evidence is distributed across all frequency bands rather than dominated by high-frequency responses, and that explicitly modeling frequency-deviation information in an anchor-relative manner significantly improves zero-shot anomaly detection performance.

title: AeroLLE: Constrained Pseudo-Supervision for Nighttime Aerial Image Enhancement with the AeroNight-1.5K Benchmark
summary: Nighttime aerial image enhancement is challenged by spatially nonuniform exposure, mixed illumination, and weak structural evidence, while registered normal-light targets are difficult to capture from moving platforms. Generated normal-light images provide practical appearance guidance but may alter geometry or texture. We introduce \aeronight{}, comprising 1,500 real nighttime aerial RGB images: 1,300 inputs are associated with manually screened pseudo-references, and 200 inputs support unpaired evaluation. We propose AeroLLE, a two-stage framework that first recovers visibility with an HVI Base Enhancer and then performs Spatially Adaptive Exposure--Color Calibration (SAECC). After the Base Enhancer is selected and frozen, SAECC predicts bounded, low-resolution RGB gain and bias fields, restricting the magnitude and spatial variation of the second-stage correction. Experiments under complementary pseudo-paired and unpaired protocols demonstrate improved agreement with screened appearance targets, together with more balanced exposure and color correction across diverse nighttime aerial scenes. These results support constrained, stage-specific calibration as a practical strategy for learning from generated appearance guidance when registered aerial references are unavailable.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces AeroNight, a benchmark of 1,500 real nighttime aerial RGB images with pseudo-references and unpaired evaluation subsets, along with AeroLLE, a two-stage framework combining an HVI Base Enhancer with Spatially Adaptive Exposure-Color Calibration (SAECC) that applies bounded, low-resolution gain/bias fields to constrain second-stage corrections when learning from generated appearance guidance.
AI.motivation: Nighttime aerial image enhancement is difficult due to spatially nonuniform exposure, mixed illumination, and weak structural evidence. Registered normal-light targets cannot be easily captured from moving aerial platforms, and generated normal-light images may alter geometry or texture, making learning from them unreliable.
AI.method: AeroLLE is a two-stage framework. First, an HVI (Hyperspectral Vegetation Index-style or Hue-Value-Intensity?) Base Enhancer recovers visibility and is selected then frozen. Second, SAECC predicts bounded, low-resolution RGB gain and bias fields, restricting the magnitude and spatial variation of the correction to avoid overfitting to noisy generated targets.
AI.result: Experiments under complementary pseudo-paired and unpaired protocols show improved agreement with screened appearance targets and more balanced exposure and color correction across diverse nighttime aerial scenes, validating the constrained, stage-specific calibration strategy.
AI.conclusion: Constrained, stage-specific calibration is a practical and effective strategy for learning from generated appearance guidance when registered aerial references are unavailable, supported by the new AeroNight benchmark.

title: Coverage-Driven Adaptive Keyframe Selection for Video Understanding
summary: Recent advances in large vision-language models (LVLMs) have enabled long-video understanding and analysis. However, processing the large number of frames in a video incurs substantial computational overhead. Existing methods reduce LVLM inference costs by scoring frame-query relevance before inference and selecting keyframes accordingly. Nevertheless, the distribution of relevant frames varies across queries, and these methods often need to score hundreds or thousands of frames. To address this limitation, we propose CSES, a training-free semantic keyframe selector that adaptively determines the numbers of frames to score and keyframes to select. CSES estimates the prominence of the frame-query relevance profile to guide active acquisition and adapt the temporal coverage of each input. It then formulates keyframe selection as a coverage problem that jointly accounts for semantic relevance, temporal redundancy, and visual redundancy. Active acquisition and keyframe selection terminate based on coverage saturation. The selection objective is monotone and submodular, enabling greedy optimization with a standard approximation guarantee. Experiments with four LVLMs on two benchmarks show that our method preserves accuracy while scoring $4$-$13\times$ fewer frames and selecting $18.4\%$-$20.5\%$ fewer input keyframes than existing baselines. CSES further achieves a $3.1$-$5.4\times$ speedup in frame selection over baselines.

AI.tldr: CSES is a training-free semantic keyframe selector for long-video LVLMs that adaptively determines how many frames to score and select, using a coverage-based formulation that jointly accounts for semantic relevance, temporal redundancy, and visual redundancy, reducing frame scoring by 4-13x and keyframe selection by 18.4-20.5% while preserving accuracy.
AI.motivation: Processing long videos with large vision-language models incurs substantial computational cost. Existing keyframe selection methods reduce costs by scoring frame-query relevance beforehand, but they often need to score hundreds or thousands of frames regardless of query-specific variability in frame relevance distribution, leading to unnecessary computation.
AI.method: CSES estimates the prominence of the frame-query relevance profile to guide active acquisition and adapt temporal coverage per input. It formulates keyframe selection as a coverage problem jointly accounting for semantic relevance, temporal redundancy, and visual redundancy. Active acquisition and keyframe selection terminate based on coverage saturation, with the objective being monotone and submodular for greedy optimization with a standard approximation guarantee.
AI.result: Experiments with four LVLMs on two benchmarks show CSES preserves accuracy while scoring 4-13x fewer frames and selecting 18.4%-20.5% fewer input keyframes than existing baselines. CSES achieves a 3.1-5.4x speedup in frame selection over baselines.
AI.conclusion: CSES demonstrates that adaptive, query-aware keyframe selection with coverage saturation can substantially reduce computational overhead in long-video LVLM inference without sacrificing accuracy, offering both efficiency gains in frame scoring and keyframe selection.

title: Generated Images Are Easier to Forget: A Machine Unlearning Perspective for Synthetic Image Detection
summary: Robust detection of generated images is critical to counter the misuse of generative models. Existing methods primarily depend on learning from human-annotated training datasets, limiting their generalization to unseen distributions. In contrast, large-scale vision models (LVMs) pre-trained on web-scale datasets exhibit exceptional generalization power through exposure to diverse distributions, offering a transformative paradigm for this task. However, our experimental results reveal that LVMs pre-trained on natural-image-dominated data can effectively capture the features of both natural and generated images, yielding comparably low losses and thus limited discriminative capacity between them. This prompts a key question: When and how do LVMs exhibit different behaviors when capturing features of natural and generated images? This investigation reveals an insight: during unlearning, LVMs exhibit disparate forgetting dynamics with feature degradation for generated images escalating faster than natural ones. Inspired by the disparate dynamics, we introduce two detection methods: 1) data-free detection, which prunes model parameters to induce unlearning without data access, and 2) data-driven detection, which optimizes LVMs to unlearn knowledge tied to generated images. Extensive experiments conducted on various benchmarks demonstrate that our unlearning-based approach outperforms conventional detection methods. By recasting the detection task as a problem of machine unlearning, our work establishes a new paradigm for generated image detection.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a novel paradigm for generated image detection by recasting it as a machine unlearning problem. The authors observe that during unlearning, large vision models (LVMs) forget generated images faster than natural ones, and leverage this disparate forgetting dynamics to build two detection methods: a data-free approach via parameter pruning and a data-driven approach via optimized unlearning.
AI.motivation: Existing generated image detection methods rely on human-annotated training data, limiting generalization to unseen distributions. LVMs pre-trained on web-scale data show exceptional generalization but fail to effectively discriminate between natural and generated images because both yield comparably low losses. This motivates investigating when and how LVM behaviors differ between natural and generated image feature capture, leading to the discovery of disparate unlearning dynamics.
AI.method: The paper proposes two detection methods based on the observed insight that during unlearning, generated images degrade faster than natural ones: (1) a data-free detection method that prunes model parameters to induce unlearning without requiring data access, and (2) a data-driven detection method that optimizes LVMs to unlearn knowledge specifically tied to generated images.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across various benchmarks demonstrate that the unlearning-based approach outperforms conventional detection methods for generated image detection.
AI.conclusion: By reframing generated image detection as a machine unlearning problem rather than a classification problem, this work establishes a new paradigm that leverages the differential forgetting dynamics of LVMs for more robust and generalizable detection.

title: Foveated Probes Recover Localized Binding Information in Vision Foundation Models
summary: Frozen vision foundation models are commonly evaluated through a single global image embedding, but this interface can conflate missing information with information lost at readout time. We study this distinction by keeping a pretrained vision encoder frozen and varying only the readout applied to its final patch tokens. We compare standard global readouts against a lightweight foveated readout, which attention-pools patch tokens using a learned or question-conditioned query, and against an oracle readout with access to the annotated target region. We evaluate these interfaces on three localized binding problems: a controlled synthetic color--shape binding task under clutter, a color-free crowded shape-detection variant, and a GQA-derived natural-image task where paired questions ask for the colors of different same-category objects in the same image. Global readouts perform near perfectly when the synthetic target appears alone, but collapse under clutter and counterfactual target edits, whereas the foveated readout recovers most of the oracle-accessible signal. On the GQA-derived task, question-independent global image vectors improve only modestly over question-only priors, while question-conditioned foveation substantially improves paired localized color accuracy. A counterfactual nuisance-to-signal ratio explains the synthetic failures: global pooling dilutes localized label-changing evidence while exposing the probe to nuisance variation from irrelevant objects. These results indicate that apparent spatial blindness in frozen vision models can arise from the global embedding interface rather than from an absence of spatial information in the frozen patch tokens.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether apparent spatial blindness in frozen vision foundation models stems from the global embedding interface rather than from missing spatial information in patch tokens. By varying only the readout applied to frozen patch tokens, they show that a lightweight foveated readout (learned or question-conditioned attention pooling) recovers most of the oracle-accessible signal on localized binding tasks, while global readouts fail under clutter, counterfactual edits, and natural-image question answering.
AI.motivation: Standard evaluation of frozen vision models uses a single global image embedding, which conflates missing spatial information with information that is present in patch tokens but lost at readout time. The authors aim to disentangle these two failure sources.
AI.method: Keep a pretrained vision encoder frozen and vary only the readout applied to final patch tokens. Compare (1) standard global readouts, (2) a lightweight foveated readout using attention pooling with learned or question-conditioned queries, and (3) an oracle readout with access to annotated target regions. Evaluate on three localized binding tasks: synthetic color-shape binding under clutter, color-free crowded shape detection, and a GQA-derived natural-image task with paired same-category object color questions. A counterfactual nuisance-to-signal ratio is proposed to explain failures.
AI.result: Global readouts perform near perfectly when targets appear alone but collapse under clutter and counterfactual edits. The foveated readout recovers most of the oracle-accessible signal. On GQA-derived tasks, global vectors improve only modestly over question-only priors, while question-conditioned foveation substantially improves paired localized color accuracy. The nuisance-to-signal ratio explains synthetic failures: global pooling dilutes localized evidence while exposing probes to irrelevant object variation.
AI.conclusion: Spatial blindness in frozen vision models can arise from the global embedding interface rather than an absence of spatial information in frozen patch tokens. Choosing an appropriate readout can recover substantial localized information without fine-tuning the encoder.

title: MDTD-ArtIR: Benchmarking Image Editing and Restoration Models for Art Image Restoration under Texture-Overlay Degradations
comment: 15 pages, 6 figures, 6 tables. Preprint submitted to Elsevier Journal of Visual Communication and Image Representation
summary: Restoring severely degraded visual media still remains a formidable challenge, as existing methods often hallucinate unnatural textures and contents, struggle with preserving color and texture, or fail to leverage partially retained image information. Existing restoration benchmarks assume known degradation operators and fail to capture the complex characteristics of artistic damage such as cracks, stains, and color/texture deviation. We introduce a controlled benchmark for blind restoration of semantic, semi-transparent image media degradations, accompanied by a new, publicly open degradation alpha texture mask dataset MDTD-Art. We present a new dataset and benchmark evaluating state-of-the-art universal restoration models against image editing and vision-language models across varying mask opacity levels. Our experiments demonstrate that image editing models consistently outperform specialized restoration architectures for arbitrary degradations, with performance gains amplified by structured prompt engineering emphasizing detail preservation and structural consistency. These findings position recoverable semantic information and prompt controllability as critical factors in art image restoration.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a controlled benchmark for blind restoration of semantic, semi-transparent image media degradations and a new dataset (MDTD-Art) with degradation alpha texture masks. It evaluates existing restoration, image editing, and vision-language models across varying mask opacity levels, finding that image editing models with structured prompts outperform specialized restoration architectures.
AI.motivation: Existing restoration methods hallucinate unnatural textures, struggle with color/texture preservation, or fail to exploit partially retained image information. Existing benchmarks assume known degradation operators and do not capture the complex characteristics of artistic damage such as cracks, stains, and color/texture deviation.
AI.method: The authors create a controlled benchmark for blind restoration of semantic/semi-transparent degradations, release a new public degradation alpha texture mask dataset (MDTD-Art), and systematically evaluate state-of-the-art universal restoration models alongside image editing and vision-language models across varying mask opacity levels, including structured prompt engineering strategies.
AI.result: Image editing models consistently outperform specialized restoration architectures for arbitrary degradations. Performance gains are amplified by structured prompt engineering that emphasizes detail preservation and structural consistency.
AI.conclusion: Recoverable semantic information and prompt controllability are critical factors in art image restoration, positioning them as key considerations for future restoration approaches.

title: LUT: Latent Utility Training for Visual Reasoning
summary: Multimodal large language models have advanced visual understanding, yet perception-intensive reasoning remains challenging. Recent latent visual reasoning methods introduce hidden-space computation before answering, but they often rely on costly intermediate supervision, such as bounding boxes, sketches, or interleaved rationales. These strategies focus on how latent states should be shaped, but do not explicitly assess whether the latent is useful for the final answer. We propose LUT, a latent reasoning framework trained with only standard VQA pairs. LUT centers training on Latent Utility at two levels. At the trajectory level, we propose Utility-Aware Latent Distillation SFT, which explores answer-relevant latent trajectories, selects qualified trajectories by their information gain, and distills more reliable and learnable supervision through curriculum learning. At the step level, we propose Latent Attribution Policy Optimization, which uses answer-to-latent attribution to differentially optimize latent steps during reinforcement learning. Experiments on perception-intensive visual reasoning benchmarks show that LUT outperforms previous latent reasoning methods and remains competitive with latent-text interleaved methods with lower annotation cost.

AI.tldr: LUT is a latent reasoning framework for multimodal LLMs trained with only standard VQA pairs, using a two-level "Latent Utility" approach: Utility-Aware Latent Distillation SFT at the trajectory level and Latent Attribution Policy Optimization at the step level, outperforming prior latent reasoning methods on perception-intensive benchmarks without costly intermediate supervision.
AI.motivation: Perception-intensive reasoning remains challenging for multimodal LLMs. Prior latent visual reasoning methods require costly intermediate supervision (bounding boxes, sketches, rationales) and focus on shaping latent states without explicitly assessing whether the latent is useful for the final answer.
AI.method: LUT introduces a two-level latent utility training framework using only standard VQA pairs: (1) Trajectory level - Utility-Aware Latent Distillation SFT selects answer-relevant latent trajectories by information gain and distills reliable supervision via curriculum learning; (2) Step level - Latent Attribution Policy Optimization uses answer-to-latent attribution for differential optimization of latent steps during RL.
AI.result: LUT outperforms previous latent reasoning methods on perception-intensive visual reasoning benchmarks and remains competitive with latent-text interleaved methods while requiring lower annotation cost.
AI.conclusion: Training latent reasoning on answer utility (rather than intermediate supervision) is effective, achieving strong performance with only standard VQA data.

title: NISF++: Geometrically-grounded implicit representations of 3D+time cardiac function from 2D short- and long-axis MR views
summary: Clinical acquisition in cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging involves obtaining cross-sectional planes of the heart along the radial and longitudinal directions. Despite these planes being 2D cross-sectional images of the heart, radiologists understand the 3D spatial and continuous temporal nature of the organ being imaged. The same can not be said about the conventional deep learning architectures used to process CMR images, which rely on in-plane and grid-based operations, and are hence unable to organically integrate information from all imaging planes. This paper builds upon previous work on neural implicit segmentation functions (NISF) to overcome unaddressed challenges in cardiac function modeling in the CMR domain. For a given subject, our architecture builds a shared 3D+time representations from all available acquisition planes regardless of orientation. By design, predictions along any imaging plane orientation are cross-sections of the same 3D representation, leading to spatio-temporal consistency across all slices. Moreover, our architecture makes the rotation and translation parameters of imaging planes learnable, allowing us to correct for the commonplace respiratory and patient motion between slice acquisitions under a rigid assumption. Furthermore, interpolation of intensities and segmentation can be performed in 4D at any desired resolution. We perform our study on a 120 subject sub-cohort of CMR imaging data from the UK-Biobank. Our in-plane segmentation performance is on-par with existing CMR segmentation methods and explore how the majority of failure cases arise from limitations in the ground-truth segmentation, for which our representations make predictions with better anatomical accuracy than its original training data. We also evaluate our motion-correction capabilities, displaying quantitative and qualitative improvements in slice alignment.

AI.tldr: A neural implicit segmentation function (NISF) based architecture for cardiac MRI that builds a shared 3D+time representation from all acquisition planes, provides spatio-temporal consistency across slices, learns plane orientation parameters to correct motion artifacts, and enables 4D intensity/segmentation interpolation at arbitrary resolution.
AI.motivation: Conventional deep learning architectures for CMR rely on in-plane and grid-based operations, failing to organically integrate information from multiple imaging planes, despite radiologists naturally understanding the 3D spatial and continuous temporal nature of the heart from 2D cross-sectional images.
AI.method: Builds upon neural implicit segmentation functions (NISF) to construct a shared 3D+time representation from all available acquisition planes regardless of orientation. Makes rotation and translation parameters of imaging planes learnable to correct for respiratory and patient motion under a rigid assumption. Interpolates intensities and segmentations in 4D at any desired resolution.
AI.result: In-plane segmentation performance is on-par with existing CMR segmentation methods on a 120-subject UK-Biobank sub-cohort. Most failure cases arise from ground-truth labeling limitations, where the representations show better anatomical accuracy than the training data. Motion correction demonstrates quantitative and qualitative improvements in slice alignment.
AI.conclusion: The proposed architecture achieves spatio-temporal consistency across CMR imaging planes, corrects motion artifacts via learnable plane parameters, and produces anatomically accurate predictions—even surpassing the quality of its own training annotations—while matching the performance of existing segmentation methods.

title: ChordVideo: One-Step, Training-Free, Temporally Consistent Video Editing via Low-Energy Transport
summary: One-step text-to-image models enable training-free, inversion-free editing with only 1--2 network function evaluations (NFE), while ChordEdit stabilizes such edits through low-energy smoothing along sampling time. Applied independently to video frames, however, it produces temporal flicker and edit-strength drift. We introduce \textbf{ChordVideo}, which extends the same low-energy principle to video time through shared noise, motion-aligned causal aggregation of per-frame Chord fields, and an optional temporally smoothed proximal correction. We derive a warping-error bound that separates motion bias from stochastic flicker and predicts diminishing returns with larger temporal windows. On TGVE/DAVIS with two one-step backbones, ChordVideo reduces warping error by \textbf{78\%} and flicker by \textbf{49\%}, improves CLIP frame consistency by \textbf{9--10 points}, and increases background PSNR by about \textbf{1.5,dB}, while retaining \textbf{2 NFE/frame}. Compared with seven multi-step editors, it achieves competitive temporal consistency and source preservation using \textbf{10--60$\times$ fewer model steps per clip

AI.tldr: ChordVideo extends the training-free, inversion-free one-step text-to-image editing paradigm (ChordEdit) to video by imposing low-energy smoothing along both sampling time and video time. It uses shared noise, motion-aligned causal aggregation of per-frame Chord fields, and optional temporally smoothed proximal correction to achieve stable, flicker-free video edits at only 2 NFE/frame.
AI.motivation: Applying one-step editing methods like ChordEdit independently to video frames causes temporal flicker and edit-strength drift, undermining temporal consistency in video editing.
AI.method: ChordVideo extends the low-energy principle of ChordEdit to video time through three components: (1) shared noise across frames, (2) motion-aligned causal aggregation of per-frame Chord fields, and (3) an optional temporally smoothed proximal correction. The authors also derive a warping-error bound separating motion bias from stochastic flicker.
AI.result: On TGVE/DAVIS with two one-step backbones, ChordVideo reduces warping error by 78%, flicker by 49%, improves CLIP frame consistency by 9-10 points, and increases background PSNR by ~1.5 dB, all while retaining 2 NFE/frame. It achieves competitive temporal consistency and source preservation versus seven multi-step editors using 10-60x fewer model steps per clip.
AI.conclusion: ChordVideo demonstrates that the low-energy editing principle can be effectively extended from single images to video, achieving strong temporal consistency and source preservation at a fraction of the computational cost of multi-step video editors.

title: CADENA: Stepwise CAD Reverse Engineering
summary: Computer-Aided Design (CAD) underpins modern engineering, yet converting existing shapes into editable models still demands substantial expert effort. Most AI systems emit the entire CAD program in a single pass, never inspecting the intermediate geometry. In contrast, human engineers build a part feature by feature, checking after each operation what remains to be modeled. We introduce CADENA (Spanish for "chain"), a model that reconstructs a 3D mesh as a parametric CAD program, growing its sequence of operations one at a time and comparing the target with the currently predicted geometry at every step. We also address the lack of benchmarks for evaluating reverse-engineering methods on mechanical parts, introducing CADENA-Bench, a benchmark that measures performance across categories of mechanical parts. CADENA outperforms prior methods on CADENA-Bench and on the DeepCAD, Fusion 360, and MCB datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/zhemdi/cadena, model weights at https://huggingface.co/kulibinai/cadena, and CADENA-Bench at https://huggingface.co/datasets/kulibinai/cadena-bench.

AI.tldr: CADENA reconstructs 3D meshes into editable parametric CAD programs by generating operations one at a time, inspecting intermediate geometry at each step, and outperforms prior methods across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Converting existing shapes into editable CAD models requires substantial expert effort. Current AI systems generate the entire CAD program in a single pass without inspecting intermediate geometry, unlike human engineers who build features incrementally and check progress after each operation.
AI.method: CADENA grows the sequence of CAD operations one at a time, comparing the target mesh with the currently predicted geometry at each step. It also introduces CADENA-Bench, a new benchmark for evaluating reverse-engineering methods on mechanical parts across categories.
AI.result: CADENA outperforms prior methods on CADENA-Bench as well as on the DeepCAD, Fusion 360, and MCB datasets.
AI.conclusion: Iterative, geometry-aware generation of CAD programs improves reverse engineering performance, and the new benchmark enables standardized evaluation of such methods on mechanical parts.

title: AIMold: An Autonomous AI-based Pipeline for Complex Mold Design
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026. Code is available at https://github.com/tb2-sy/AIMold
summary: Injection molding is the cornerstone of mass-producing plastic components. While current algorithms can automate mold design for basic geometries using standard two-piece molds, complex parts featuring undercuts, side holes, or re-entrant features present a significant challenge. These geometries often necessitate auxiliary components beyond the primary upper and lower molds. In practice, designing these intricate assemblies is a laborious process that relies heavily on expert knowledge. Furthermore, the scarcity of public datasets has hindered the development of effective learning-based solutions. To bridge these gaps, we introduce MoldCAD, a curated dataset that pairs complex single-body CAD parts with industry-standard mold assemblies. Each entry includes the upper and lower molds, parting surfaces, demolding orientations, and necessary auxiliary components. The dataset comprises 4,934 CAD models and over 3,850 mold assemblies, totaling more than 23k individual models. Building upon this dataset, we propose a comprehensive pipeline that predicts demolding orientations, identifies auxiliary components, and constructs parting surfaces to derive a complete, manufacturing-ready mold assembly for downstream CAD/CAM workflows. Our results demonstrate a promising path toward fully automated industrial mold design and contribute to the broader advancement of manufacturing-aware CAD generation.

AI.tldr: MoldCAD is a curated dataset of 4,934 CAD models paired with 3,850+ industry-standard mold assemblies (23k+ individual models) for complex plastic parts with undercuts and re-entrant features. It also proposes a pipeline that predicts demolding orientations, identifies auxiliary components, and constructs parting surfaces to generate manufacturing-ready mold assemblies.
AI.motivation: Injection mold design for complex parts (with undercuts, side holes, re-entrant features) is laborious and expert-dependent, unlike basic geometries which are already automated. The scarcity of public datasets has also blocked learning-based approaches.
AI.method: Introduces MoldCAD, a large-scale dataset pairing complex single-body CAD parts with industry-standard mold assemblies (upper/lower molds, parting surfaces, demolding orientations, auxiliary components). Proposes a comprehensive pipeline predicting demolding orientations, identifying auxiliary components, and constructing parting surfaces to produce complete mold assemblies.
AI.result: Dataset contains 4,934 CAD models, 3,850+ mold assemblies, totaling over 23k individual models. The pipeline demonstrates a promising path toward fully automated industrial mold design.
AI.conclusion: The work shows a promising direction for fully automated mold design and contributes to manufacturing-aware CAD generation, addressing both the dataset scarcity and automation challenges in complex mold design.

title: Models as Tools: An Agentic Coordination Framework for Unified Multimodal Visual Tracking
summary: Most current visual trackers adopt a matching-based architecture trained exclusively on tracking datasets, whose performance gains depend heavily on the length of the input context, and have now reached a bottleneck. While high-performance tracking increasingly relies on foundation models, existing methods use them monolithically, adapting a foundation model into a tracker or modify a segmentation foundation model into a tracking pipeline, which fails to exploit complementary strengths. Matching-based trackers excel at instance-level correspondence but lack semantic discrimination and fine-grained foreground perception, whereas segmentation foundation models produce precise masks yet struggle with instance discrimination and multimodal extension. Both paradigms also lack error-correction capabilities for long-term tracking. To address these issues, we propose ACTrack, an agentic coordination framework that treats heterogeneous models as invocable tools under an event-triggered mechanism. ACTrack coordinates a Tracker-based Instance Matching Tool for target discrimination, a SAM3 Motion Tool for mask-derived motion priors, a SAM3 Perception Tool for detecting distractors and instance-conflict cues, and a VLM Reprompt Tool activated only under persistent conflict to mitigate error accumulation. We design a complete tool-invocation trigger mechanism and an inter-tool coordination mechanism, enabling the complementary strengths of different model tools to be fully integrated. Experiments show that ACTrack substantially surpasses the strongest and the largest trackers on eight RGB benchmarks. Furthermore, a parameter-efficient adaptation strategy enables parameter sharing and reuse across tools, achieving unified multimodal tracking with only 30\% trainable parameters while substantially outperforming prior methods on multimodal benchmarks such as LasHeR, VisEvent, TNL2K, and DepthTrack.

AI.tldr: ACTrack is an agentic coordination framework that treats heterogeneous models (tracking, segmentation, vision-language) as invocable tools under an event-triggered mechanism, achieving state-of-the-art results on eight RGB benchmarks and unified multimodal tracking with only 30% trainable parameters.
AI.motivation: Matching-based trackers suffer from lack of semantic discrimination and fine-grained foreground perception, while segmentation foundation models lack instance discrimination and multimodal extension. Both paradigms lack error-correction for long-term tracking, and existing foundation-model-based methods use them monolithically rather than exploiting complementary strengths.
AI.method: ACTrack coordinates four tools: a Tracker-based Instance Matching Tool for target discrimination, a SAM3 Motion Tool for mask-derived motion priors, a SAM3 Perception Tool for distractor detection, and a VLM Reprompt Tool activated under persistent conflict. It includes a complete tool-invocation trigger mechanism and inter-tool coordination, plus a parameter-efficient adaptation strategy enabling parameter sharing across tools.
AI.result: ACTrack substantially surpasses the strongest and largest trackers on eight RGB benchmarks, and outperforms prior methods on multimodal benchmarks (LasHeR, VisEvent, TNL2K, DepthTrack) with only 30% trainable parameters.
AI.conclusion: By treating heterogeneous models as coordinated tools with event-triggered invocation, ACTrack effectively integrates complementary strengths of different model paradigms and addresses the error-accumulation problem, achieving state-of-the-art performance across RGB and multimodal tracking benchmarks with high parameter efficiency.

title: MIDAL: Math Image Descriptions for Accessible Learning
summary: Many open educational resources are lacking in accessibility, especially in-depth image descriptions. In subjects like Science and Mathematics, however, it can be particularly difficult to write image descriptions since there can be many complicated expressions and names depending upon the course level. To help fill that gap in a small way, we introduce Math Image Descriptions for Accessible Learning (MIDAL), a math image-description dataset of 2,020 mathematical images spanning multiple educational levels, to aid in training vision language models to create image descriptions following accessibility best practices. We hope MIDAL is a valuable resource in enhancing the conversation and innovation regarding accessibility of STEM content in higher education. This dataset is however not just limited in math description generation but can also be used to fine-tune language models that can have improved mathematical reasoning and answers.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MIDAL (Math Image Descriptions for Accessible Learning), a dataset of 2,020 mathematical images spanning multiple educational levels, designed to train vision language models to generate accessible image descriptions for STEM educational resources, particularly benefiting visually impaired learners.
AI.motivation: Many open educational resources lack accessibility, especially in-depth image descriptions. Science and Mathematics content is particularly challenging because of complicated expressions and domain-specific terminology that varies by course level.
AI.method: The authors create MIDAL, a curated dataset of 2,020 mathematical images across multiple educational levels, annotated with image descriptions that follow accessibility best practices for training vision language models.
AI.result: The MIDAL dataset is introduced as a resource for training vision language models to generate accessible image descriptions and also for fine-tuning language models to improve mathematical reasoning and answer generation.
AI.conclusion: MIDAL serves as a valuable resource for advancing accessibility research and innovation in STEM higher education content, with broader applications beyond description generation to mathematical reasoning tasks.

title: PhenoStitch: Training-Free Panoptic Crop Mapping from Satellite Image Time Series
summary: Panoptic crop mapping requires both delineating individual agricultural parcels and assigning a crop type to each parcel from satellite image time series. Existing approaches typically rely on dense parcel-level annotations and task-specific model training, which limits their applicability to new regions and growing seasons. We introduce PhenoStitch, a panoptic crop-mapping pipeline that requires no task-specific gradient-based training. A frozen Segment Anything model first oversegments each patch into class-agnostic regions. For each region, optical NDVI and Sentinel-1 backscatter series are summarized by an analytic double-harmonic phenological signature. Adjacent regions are then merged into parcels by minimizing a Potts graph energy, and each parcel is classified by nearest-prototype matching using only (k) labeled parcels per class. A final topology-closure step produces the panoptic map. Under a matched budget of (k=20) parcels per class, corresponding to less than 1% of the available labels, PhenoStitch achieves 20.0 crop mIoU, 76.2 segmentation quality, and 6.2 panoptic quality on PASTIS-R under a 5-fold, 3-seed evaluation. It outperforms the evaluated frozen foundation-model, few-shot, and matched-budget supervised baselines under the same protocol, with a consistent ranking also observed on ZueriCrop. Ablation studies show that radar observations contribute the largest performance gain, while the graph-energy merge and compact phenological signature provide further improvements. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining label-free parcel delineation with few-shot phenological recognition for panoptic crop mapping under limited supervision.

AI.tldr: PhenoStitch is a panoptic crop-mapping pipeline requiring no task-specific gradient-based training. It uses a frozen Segment Anything model for oversegmentation, summarizes phenological signatures (optical NDVI + Sentinel-1 backscatter) with analytic double-harmonic functions, merges regions via Potts graph energy, and classifies parcels via nearest-prototype matching with minimal labels. It outperforms frozen foundation-model, few-shot, and matched-budget supervised baselines on PASTIS-R and ZueriCrop.
AI.motivation: Existing panoptic crop-mapping approaches rely on dense parcel-level annotations and task-specific training, limiting scalability to new regions and growing seasons. The goal is to enable effective panoptic crop mapping with minimal supervision and without task-specific gradient-based training.
AI.method: A frozen SAM oversegments patches into class-agnostic regions. For each region, optical NDVI and Sentinel-1 backscatter series are summarized via an analytic double-harmonic phenological signature. Adjacent regions are merged into parcels by minimizing Potts graph energy. Parcels are classified via nearest-prototype matching using k labeled parcels per class. A final topology-closure step produces the panoptic map.
AI.result: With k=20 parcels per class (<1% labels), PhenoStitch achieves 20.0 crop mIoU, 76.2 segmentation quality, and 6.2 panoptic quality on PASTIS-R (5-fold, 3-seed). It outperforms frozen foundation-model, few-shot, and matched-budget supervised baselines. Radar observations contribute the largest performance gain; graph-energy merging and the compact phenological signature provide further improvements. Consistent ranking on ZueriCrop.
AI.conclusion: Combining label-free parcel delineation with few-shot phenological recognition is effective for panoptic crop mapping under limited supervision, demonstrating a generalizable and annotation-efficient alternative to fully supervised approaches.

title: MBO Scheme for Local Chan--Vese Segmentation
comment: Accepted to Image Processing On Line; Github link to code: https://github.com/kbui1993/Official_LCV_Code
summary: Robust to intensity inhomogeneity, the local Chan--Vese (LCV) model extends the classical Chan--Vese (CV) image segmentation method by incorporating local statistical information around each pixel. Originally, the LCV model was solved using a finite difference scheme, following the approach used for the CV model. As an alternative to the finite difference scheme, a more efficient algorithm based on the Merriman-Bence-Osher (MBO) scheme was later developed for the CV model. In this paper, we derive a similar MBO-based algorithm to solve the LCV model and propose an efficient implementation. The algorithm is developed for both two-phase and multiphase segmentation, and an extension to color images is also discussed. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, we apply it to a variety of grayscale and color images, including medical and microscopy images.

AI.tldr: This paper develops an MBO (Merriman-Bence-Osher) scheme-based algorithm to solve the Local Chan-Vese (LCV) image segmentation model, providing an efficient alternative to the original finite difference approach. The method supports two-phase, multiphase, and color image segmentation, and is validated on grayscale, color, medical, and microscopy images.
AI.motivation: The LCV model improves upon the classical CV model by incorporating local statistical information to handle intensity inhomogeneity. However, its original finite difference solver is computationally expensive. Since an MBO-based algorithm proved more efficient for the CV model, the authors aim to derive a similar MBO-based approach for the LCV model to achieve faster and more efficient segmentation.
AI.method: The authors derive an MBO-based algorithm to solve the LCV model, adapted from the MBO scheme previously developed for the CV model. The algorithm is designed for both two-phase and multiphase segmentation, with an additional extension to color images. An efficient implementation of the proposed MBO-LCV algorithm is provided.
AI.result: The proposed MBO-based LCV algorithm is applied to a variety of grayscale and color images, including medical and microscopy images, demonstrating its effectiveness for image segmentation tasks.
AI.conclusion: The MBO-based algorithm provides an efficient alternative to finite difference solving of the LCV model, extending its applicability to two-phase, multiphase, and color image segmentation while maintaining robustness to intensity inhomogeneity.

title: PeCA: Palette Context Assisted Inference for Test-Time Paint-Bucket Colourisation on Animation Videos
summary: In animation production, paint-bucket colourisation for hand-drawn animation is a labour-intensive procedure that assigns each enclosed region in line sketches a colour from reference design sheets. Recent automatic paint-bucket colourisation pipelines mirror this workflow via region correspondence, but correspondences can be brittle when regions are ambiguous fragments without proper context. In this paper, we propose Palette Context Assisted (PeCA), a new training-free, plug-and-play framework for animation video colourisation that aims to close this gap at test-time via reasoning over spatial and temporal contexts. Extensive experiments on existing benchmarks and a newly introduced long-video test case show consistent performance boosts.

AI.tldr: PeCA is a training-free, plug-and-play framework for animation video colourisation that improves automatic paint-bucket colourisation by reasoning over spatial and temporal contexts at test-time, yielding consistent performance gains on benchmarks and long-video test cases.
AI.motivation: Automatic paint-bucket colourisation for hand-drawn animation relies on region correspondence, but these correspondences are brittle when regions are ambiguous fragments lacking proper context. This limits accuracy and robustness in real animation workflows.
AI.method: A training-free, plug-and-play framework called Palette Context Assisted (PeCA) that closes the gap at test-time by reasoning over both spatial and temporal contexts to resolve ambiguous region correspondences.
AI.result: Consistent performance boosts are demonstrated on existing benchmarks and a newly introduced long-video test case.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating spatial and temporal context reasoning at test-time meaningfully improves automatic paint-bucket colourisation without requiring additional training.

title: Look Up and Look Back: Hidden Attention and Latent Orientation in a Frozen Foundation Model for Panoramic SLAM
summary: Monocular panoramic SLAM benefits from substantial visual overlap under large camera rotations, yet remains prone to errors caused by camera tilt, scale drift, and false loop closures. We show that a frozen panoramic geometry foundation model provides useful internal cues beyond its explicit geometric outputs: intermediate tokens encode gravity in the camera frame, while cross-view attention provides a compatibility cue for potential revisits. Building on these cues, we present HALO-SLAM. A gravity readout enables IMU-free spherical upright canonicalization. For loop closure, we introduce a cost-aware three-stage cascade combining DBoW2 event-level retrieval, attention-based compatibility filtering, and dense geometric validation through symmetric submap augmentation. Accepted revisits yield pixel-aligned 3D--3D correspondences in both local gauges, from which robust $\mathrm{Sim}(3)$ constraints are estimated and jointly optimized with sequential constraints in a global pose graph. Across 125 sequences from five real-world panoramic benchmarks, our method achieves \textbf{100\%} sequence success (\textbf{125/125}) under the stated criterion and the lowest ATE among the evaluated methods on all five benchmarks, reducing ATE by \textbf{30--88\%} relative to the best ERP-native baseline on each benchmark.

AI.tldr: HALO-SLAM is a monocular panoramic SLAM system that leverages a frozen panoramic geometry foundation model for gravity estimation and loop closure, achieving 100% sequence success (125/125) and the lowest ATE across five real-world benchmarks, with 30-88% ATE reduction.
AI.motivation: Monocular panoramic SLAM suffers from errors caused by camera tilt, scale drift, and false loop closures despite benefiting from large visual overlap under big rotations.
AI.method: HALO-SLAM uses a frozen panoramic geometry foundation model: (1) intermediate tokens encode gravity for IMU-free spherical upright canonicalization; (2) cross-view attention provides revisit compatibility cues; (3) a cost-aware three-stage loop-closure cascade combining DBoW2 retrieval, attention-based compatibility filtering, and dense geometric validation via symmetric submap augmentation; (4) robust Sim(3) constraints from pixel-aligned 3D-3D correspondences optimized in a global pose graph with sequential constraints.
AI.result: Across 125 sequences from five real-world panoramic benchmarks, HALO-SLAM achieves 100% sequence success (125/125) and the lowest ATE on all five benchmarks, reducing ATE by 30-88% relative to the best ERP-native baseline per benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Internal cues from panoramic foundation models beyond explicit outputs significantly improve SLAM robustness and accuracy for monocular panoramic systems.

title: Swimm3R: Splatting with Medium-aware SfM for Underwater 3D Reconstruction
summary: We propose Swimm3R, a unified framework that combines medium-aware structure-from-motion (SfM) with Underwater Beta Splatting to address scattering- and attenuation-induced failures in underwater 3D reconstruction. Swimm3R distills in-air geometric priors into a feed-forward backbone and uses a physics head to regress underwater image-formation parameters, camera poses, and restored point clouds. Additionally, we introduce Underwater Beta Splatting, which extends Gaussian splatting with Beta primitives and scattering-aware geometric gradients for stable underwater geometry representation. We further establish the Barbados underwater video dataset to demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in challenging underwater environments. On this dataset, Swimm3R robustly recovers underwater scene structure under challenging scattering conditions, yielding coherent seafloor geometry. Using these predicted point clouds, the proposed Underwater Beta Splatting improves average PSNR by $1.47$ dB over WaterSplatting while increasing downstream localization performance by $2.0$ and $2.4$ percentage points in RRA@15 and RTA@15, respectively.

AI.tldr: Swimm3R is a unified framework combining medium-aware SfM with Underwater Beta Splatting to tackle scattering and attenuation issues in underwater 3D reconstruction, achieving improved PSNR and localization accuracy over prior methods.
AI.motivation: Underwater 3D reconstruction fails due to scattering and attenuation effects that degrade image quality and geometric accuracy.
AI.method: Swimm3R distills in-air geometric priors into a feed-forward backbone with a physics head to regress underwater image-formation parameters, camera poses, and point clouds. Underwater Beta Splatting extends Gaussian splatting using Beta primitives and scattering-aware geometric gradients.
AI.result: On the Barbados underwater video dataset, Swimm3R recovers coherent seafloor geometry and Underwater Beta Splatting improves average PSNR by 1.47 dB over WaterSplatting, with +2.0 and +2.4 percentage points in RRA@15 and RTA@15 localization metrics.
AI.conclusion: The proposed unified framework robustly handles challenging underwater scattering conditions, delivering better geometry reconstruction and downstream localization performance.

title: MonitorVLM-v2: A Deployed Vision-Language Framework for Real-Time Safety Violation Detection
summary: Large vision--language models (VLMs) can reason step by step about complex visual scenes, but this open-ended, autoregressive chain-of-thought (CoT) approach is poorly suited to safety-critical, rule-governed settings such as industrial surveillance, where decisions must be bounded, deterministic, and low-latency. Because CoT inference cost scales jointly with reasoning length and the number of concurrent streams, it creates a throughput bottleneck that precludes the real-time, multistream monitoring required for industrial accountability. Here we present MonitorVLM-v2, a deployment-oriented framework that recasts VLM-based safety assessment as probabilistic inference over a finite regulatory decision space, compressing multimodal reasoning into single-step rule-ID predictions and reducing decoding from a variable-length sequence to a single token. We introduce symbolic policy optimization (SymPO), a novel contrastive policy optimization algorithm that sharpens decision boundaries within this finite symbolic space, together with an entropy-driven triage mechanism that routes uncertain predictions to human reviewers for expert confirmation. In a four-month prospective deployment across 10 concurrent camera feeds in an operational underground mining facility, MonitorVLM-v2 achieved a 19.45-fold increase in inference speed and identified 2.78 times as many confirmed violations as the site's routine manual inspection workflow, demonstrating the practical value of compressed symbolic decision-making for real-time, auditable industrial monitoring.

AI.tldr: MonitorVLM-v2 is a deployment-oriented framework that reframes VLM-based safety assessment as probabilistic inference over a finite regulatory decision space, compressing multimodal reasoning into single-step rule-ID predictions. Using symbolic policy optimization (SymPO) and an entropy-driven triage mechanism, it achieved a 19.45-fold inference speedup and identified 2.78x more confirmed violations than manual inspection in a real underground mining deployment.
AI.motivation: Traditional open-ended, autoregressive chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning in VLMs is unsuitable for safety-critical, rule-governed settings like industrial surveillance because CoT inference cost grows with both reasoning length and concurrent streams, creating throughput bottlenecks that prevent real-time multistream monitoring.
AI.method: The paper introduces MonitorVLM-v2, which compresses multimodal reasoning into single-step rule-ID predictions over a finite regulatory decision space (reducing decoding from variable-length sequences to a single token). It also proposes symbolic policy optimization (SymPO), a contrastive policy optimization algorithm that sharpens decision boundaries, plus an entropy-driven triage mechanism that routes uncertain predictions to human reviewers.
AI.result: In a four-month prospective deployment across 10 concurrent camera feeds in an operational underground mining facility, MonitorVLM-v2 achieved a 19.45-fold increase in inference speed and identified 2.78 times as many confirmed violations as the site's routine manual inspection workflow.
AI.conclusion: Compressed symbolic decision-making demonstrates practical value for real-time, auditable industrial monitoring, offering a viable alternative to autoregressive CoT reasoning for safety-critical applications.

title: Location-Aware Fine-Grained Representation Learning for Medical Vision Foundation Models
summary: Fine-grained visual representations are essential for medical image analysis, particularly when diagnostically relevant evidence is subtle and spatially localized. Modern transformer-based medical vision encoders must therefore learn patch-level representations that are both clinically meaningful and spatially consistent. Without these properties, large vision-language models (LVLMs) operate on an ambiguous visual foundation, limiting their ability to generate clinically reliable and spatially grounded responses. However, existing training strategies for medical vision encoders rarely achieve both objectives. Image-text alignment provides clinically meaningful supervision primarily at the image level, leaving the spatial localization of diagnostic evidence weakly constrained. In contrast, self-supervised learning promotes spatial consistency but lacks the semantic supervision needed to distinguish visually similar yet clinically distinct regions. To address this gap, we present LoFi, a medical vision foundation model built on location-aware fine-grained representation learning. LoFi trains a vision encoder with a lightweight large language model under grounding and grounded captioning objectives. Because these objectives require predicting location from clinical text and vice versa, spatial consistency emerges without any explicit patch-level regularization. To enable training at scale, we construct MedG, a large-scale medical grounding dataset of 4.48M image-text-box triplets curated from 84 datasets spanning 7 modalities. Across phrase grounding, visual question answering, and region-based organ classification under perturbations, LoFi consistently outperforms general-purpose and medical vision foundation models as well as state-of-the-art LVLMs. Code is available at https://github.com/myeongkyunkang/lofi-medg.

AI.tldr: LoFi is a medical vision foundation model that learns location-aware fine-grained representations through grounding and grounded captioning objectives, trained on MedG, a large-scale medical grounding dataset of 4.48M image-text-box triplets across 7 modalities, achieving state-of-the-art performance in phrase grounding, VQA, and region-based classification.
AI.motivation: Existing medical vision encoders fail to simultaneously achieve clinically meaningful and spatially consistent patch-level representations. Image-text alignment provides semantic but image-level supervision, while self-supervised learning provides spatial consistency but lacks clinical semantic distinction.
AI.method: LoFi trains a vision encoder with a lightweight LLM using two objectives: grounding (predicting location from clinical text) and grounded captioning (predicting text from location). This bidirectional prediction naturally induces spatial consistency without explicit patch-level regularization. A large-scale dataset MedG (4.48M image-text-box triplets, 84 datasets, 7 modalities) enables scalable training.
AI.result: LoFi consistently outperforms general-purpose and medical vision foundation models as well as state-of-the-art LVLMs across phrase grounding, visual question answering, and region-based organ classification under perturbations.
AI.conclusion: Location-aware fine-grained representation learning simultaneously achieves clinical meaningfulness and spatial consistency in medical vision encoders, providing a stronger visual foundation for medical LVLMs.

title: Understanding and Overcoming Cross-modal Fusion Bias in Multimodal Anomaly Detection From A Fisher Information Perspective
summary: Current advancements in Multimodal Anomaly Detection (MAD) are largely driven by enhancing multimodal fusion, particularly through the integration of RGB and Depth data for richer anomaly representation. However, less attention was devoted to analyzing the role of cross-modal fusion bias, a well-known challenge in multimodal learning, in MAD. This gap motivates a key question: can we overcome this bias to break the performance bottleneck of current work? In this paper, we first analyze the impact of cross-modal fusion bias in MAD via the Fisher Information Matrix. Then, grounded in these findings, we propose UCFB, a simple yet effective plug-and-play framework designed to mitigate cross-modal fusion bias in MAD. It achieves this by jointly employing Fisher-information-guided dynamic calibration to adjust modality-specific regularization weights and canonical similarity analysis to improve inter-modal interactions. Extensive experiments on the MVTec 3D-AD and Eyecandies datasets demonstrate that UCFB achieves consistent improvements in single-class, multi-class, and few-shot settings.

AI.tldr: UCFB is a simple yet effective plug-and-play framework that mitigates cross-modal fusion bias in Multimodal Anomaly Detection (MAD) by using Fisher Information Matrix-guided dynamic calibration for modality-specific regularization and canonical similarity analysis for improved inter-modal interactions, achieving consistent improvements across multiple settings.
AI.motivation: While multimodal fusion (especially RGB and Depth integration) has driven advances in MAD, cross-modal fusion bias—a known challenge in multimodal learning—has been largely overlooked. The authors question whether overcoming this bias can break the current performance bottleneck in MAD.
AI.method: The authors first analyze cross-modal fusion bias in MAD using the Fisher Information Matrix. Based on this analysis, they propose UCFB, a plug-and-play framework that jointly employs (1) Fisher-information-guided dynamic calibration to adjust modality-specific regularization weights, and (2) canonical similarity analysis to enhance inter-modal interactions.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on MVTec 3D-AD and Eyecandies datasets demonstrate that UCFB achieves consistent improvements in single-class, multi-class, and few-shot settings.
AI.conclusion: Addressing cross-modal fusion bias via Fisher Information-guided calibration and canonical similarity analysis can effectively break the performance bottleneck in current multimodal anomaly detection methods, as validated by consistent gains across multiple experimental settings.

title: Entity-Faithful Repair of Synthetic Supervision for Zero-Shot Image Captioning
comment: Accepted to the 34th ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM 2026). 16 pages, 7 figures
summary: Zero-shot image captioning aims to generate image descriptions without annotated image-text pairs. Recent approaches exploit text-to-image models to synthesize training data from text-only corpora, but most focus on improving overall data quality. In contrast, we observe that synthetic image-text misalignment is often structured and fine-grained: pairs may remain globally plausible while containing missing entities or misgrounded attributes, thereby degrading supervision fidelity. As a result, methods based on global similarity for image rematching or regeneration may improve apparent plausibility, but cannot systematically repair entity-level misalignment. To address this issue, we propose ReCap, a plug-and-play framework that shifts synthetic data refinement from implicit global matching to explicit fine-grained realignment. Specifically, ReCap enforces entity-level correspondence by using detected image-supported entities to guide caption rewriting, yielding more faithful synthetic supervision. In addition, we introduce an adaptive dynamic weighted learning strategy to downweight unreliable synthetic pairs during training. As a general framework, ReCap can be integrated into existing synthetic-data pipelines. Extensive experiments show that ReCap consistently improves image-text consistency and achieves state-of-the-art performance on both in-domain and cross-domain zero-shot image captioning benchmarks.

AI.tldr: ReCap is a plug-and-play framework that improves zero-shot image captioning by refining synthetic training data through explicit fine-grained entity-level realignment (rather than implicit global matching), using detected image-supported entities to guide caption rewriting and an adaptive dynamic weighted learning strategy to downweight unreliable pairs.
AI.motivation: Synthetic image-text pairs generated from text-to-image models often contain structured, fine-grained misalignments (e.g., missing entities or misgrounded attributes) that remain globally plausible, and existing global similarity-based methods cannot systematically repair these entity-level errors, degrading supervision fidelity.
AI.method: ReCap shifts synthetic data refinement from implicit global matching to explicit fine-grained realignment by: (1) enforcing entity-level correspondence via detected image-supported entities to guide caption rewriting, and (2) introducing an adaptive dynamic weighted learning strategy to downweight unreliable synthetic pairs during training. It is designed as a plug-and-play framework compatible with existing synthetic-data pipelines.
AI.result: ReCap consistently improves image-text consistency and achieves state-of-the-art performance on both in-domain and cross-domain zero-shot image captioning benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Fine-grained entity-level refinement of synthetic data is more effective than global matching for improving zero-shot image captioning, and ReCap serves as a general framework that can be integrated into existing pipelines to enhance supervision fidelity.

title: Can Humans Dream of Electric Sheep? Human-Written Samples for Fine-Grained Vision-and-Language Hallucination Benchmarking
summary: In an age of rapid model turnover, how do we make hallucination evaluation more perennial? We explore whether human-written hallucination samples could take the place of model-generated hallucinations, in order to make benchmarking detection independent of particular models. To this end, we construct a dataset of 1,600 human-written samples, spanning four languages (Chinese, English, French, Italian), and 18,400 samples from five vision-and-language models, all annotated for hallucinations using a fine-grained span-level labeling scheme. We find that human-written samples result in higher agreement and allow greater control of dataset contents, while remaining distributionally similar to samples derived from vision-and-language samples and providing a reasonable portrayal of detection capabilities - suggesting that human data is a viable substitute for model-based hallucination benchmarks.

AI.tldr: This paper explores whether human-written hallucination samples can replace model-generated hallucinations for benchmarking detection systems in vision-and-language tasks, finding that human data yields higher agreement, greater control, and distributional similarity to model-derived samples, making it a viable perennial benchmark substitute.
AI.motivation: Rapid model turnover makes hallucination evaluation benchmarks quickly outdated since they depend on specific models. The authors seek a more durable, model-independent approach to benchmark hallucination detection.
AI.method: Constructed a dataset of 1,600 human-written hallucination samples across four languages (Chinese, English, French, Italian) and 18,400 samples from five vision-and-language models, annotated with a fine-grained span-level labeling scheme for hallucinations.
AI.result: Human-written samples achieve higher inter-annotator agreement, provide greater control over dataset contents, remain distributionally similar to model-derived samples, and offer a reasonable portrayal of detection capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Human-written data is a viable substitute for model-based hallucination benchmarks, enabling more perennial and model-independent evaluation of hallucination detection.

title: Struct-GStream: Towards Efficient Free-Viewpoint Video Streaming at Low-Bitrates with Structured 3D Gaussians
summary: Constructing photorealistic Free-Viewpoint Videos (FVVs) of dynamic scenes from a set of posed 2D images has been an intriguing yet challenging task in computer vision. Methods based on neural rendering achieve high-fidelity image quality in FVV construction. However, most of these methods are unable to achieve real-time rendering and often require complete video sequences to train. Despite the existence of some online training methods capable of rendering FVVs in real time, they struggle to meet the requirements for storage and training time for downstream applications. To overcome this problem, we propose Struct-GStream, which can achieve efficient FVV streaming using structured 3D Gaussians (3DGs). Specifically, we introduce dynamic anchor points to generate structured 3DGs to construct basic scenes and model approximate scene movements based on the assumption of local rigidity in object motion. Besides, we introduce a global free 3DGs patching strategy involving free 3DGs' generation, pruning, and optimization to patch and model deficient areas and emerging objects. Our method achieves fast training at low bitrates while maintaining high rendering quality. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Struct-GStream significantly outperforms existing online training methods for FVV construction in terms of training time, storage, and rendering quality while maintaining competitive rendering speed.

AI.tldr: Struct-GStream is a method for efficient free-viewpoint video streaming using structured 3D Gaussians, achieving fast training at low bitrates while maintaining high rendering quality and real-time speed.
AI.motivation: Existing neural rendering methods for Free-Viewpoint Videos (FVVs) either cannot achieve real-time rendering and require complete video sequences for training, or online training methods that support real-time FVV rendering struggle with storage and training time requirements for downstream applications.
AI.method: Struct-GStream introduces dynamic anchor points to generate structured 3D Gaussians for constructing basic scenes, models approximate scene movements using local rigidity assumptions in object motion, and employs a global free 3D Gaussians patching strategy (generation, pruning, optimization) to handle deficient areas and emerging objects.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show Struct-GStream significantly outperforms existing online training methods for FVV construction in training time, storage, and rendering quality, while maintaining competitive rendering speed.
AI.conclusion: Structured 3D Gaussians enable efficient FVV streaming by balancing fast training, low storage requirements, high rendering quality, and real-time rendering performance.

title: Credit the Right Box: Marginal Contribution Assignment for Structured Visual Perception
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly expected to solve structured perception tasks that require visual recognition, language-to-object binding, object cardinality preservation, and precisely localized grounding and segmentation outputs. However, existing group-relative reinforcement learning methods provide only response-level supervision, creating a granularity mismatch for structured multi-object prediction: a single advantage is broadcast to all tokens in a response, without distinguishing individual box contributions. To address this mismatch, we propose MCR-GRPO, a marginal contribution assignment framework that derives box-level credit directly from each sampled response. Specifically, Marginal Contribution Reward (MCR) estimates each predicted box's contribution through a leave-one-out comparison, measuring how the matched set value changes when the box is removed from the response. After within-response normalization, records that improve the set value receive positive credit, while redundant or harmful ones are suppressed. To make marginal attribution stable and informative, we further introduce a Continuous Matched Set Value Evaluator that integrates permutation-invariant matching, count-aware normalization, and graded localization. MCR-GRPO maps normalized box-level marginal advantages to the token spans that generated each box, preserving GRPO's response-level comparison while enabling box-aware optimization of structured multi-object grounding. Experiments across REC, DOD, segmentation, and counting benchmarks show state-of-the-art performance over prior GRPO-based baselines.

AI.tldr: MCR-GRPO introduces a marginal contribution assignment framework for group-relative reinforcement learning in structured multi-object perception tasks, deriving box-level credit from leave-one-out comparisons to enable fine-grained optimization of MLLMs for grounding, segmentation, and counting.
AI.motivation: Existing GRPO methods provide only response-level supervision, creating a granularity mismatch for structured multi-object prediction where a single advantage is broadcast uniformly across all tokens without distinguishing individual box contributions.
AI.method: MCR-GRPO has two key components: (1) Marginal Contribution Reward (MCR) that estimates each predicted box's contribution via leave-one-out comparison of matched set value, followed by within-response normalization; (2) a Continuous Matched Set Value Evaluator integrating permutation-invariant matching, count-aware normalization, and graded localization for stable marginal attribution. Box-level marginal advantages are mapped to token spans generating each box.
AI.result: State-of-the-art performance over prior GRPO-based baselines across referring expression comprehension (REC), detection (DOD), segmentation, and counting benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Box-level credit assignment enables granular optimization for structured multi-object grounding tasks while preserving GRPO's response-level comparison framework.

title: Extended KAFR: A kinematic-adaptive paradigm for the efficient analysis of surgical video
summary: Artificial Intelligence is increasingly applied to surgical video analysis for phase segmentation, skill assessment, and workflow optimization. A key challenge is the length of surgical recordings, often one to several hours, creating substantial computational burden. We previously developed Kinematics-Adaptive Frame Recognition (KAFR) for robotic surgery, showing that tracking tool motion effectively identifies informative frames while filtering redundant content. However, laparoscopic surgery introduces additional challenges: manual camera control causes frequent motion artifacts, and image quality is generally lower than robotic systems. This study evaluates whether KAFR generalizes to laparoscopic surgery using the Cholec80 benchmark, comprising 80 laparoscopic cholecystectomy procedures annotated for seven surgical phases. KAFR operates in three stages: a fine-tuned YOLO model detects and segments surgical tools; frames are adaptively selected based on tool displacement or velocity variation; and an X3D model classifies selected frames into surgical phases. KAFR achieved a 91.0\% F1 score using only 0.58\% of frames for phase classification, representing an approximately seven-fold reduction compared to typical 4\% frame sampling, while maintaining performance comparable to LoViT (90.2\%) and Trans-SVNet (89.7\%). These results demonstrate that kinematics-based frame selection transfers effectively to the challenging laparoscopic environment.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates whether KAFR (Kinematics-Adaptive Frame Recognition), originally developed for robotic surgery, generalizes to laparoscopic surgery. Using the Cholec80 benchmark, KAFR achieves a 91.0% F1 score using only 0.58% of frames for surgical phase classification—a ~7x reduction in frame sampling compared to typical 4% sampling—while maintaining performance comparable to existing methods.
AI.motivation: Surgical videos are extremely long (1-3 hours), creating substantial computational burden for AI-based analysis. While KAFR was previously developed for robotic surgery to filter redundant frames via tool motion tracking, laparoscopic surgery introduces additional challenges (manual camera control causing motion artifacts, lower image quality), so it is unclear whether KAFR generalizes to this more difficult domain.
